domain: Geocoding and address hierarchy (free-text address -> lat/lon -> nested place names with OSM ids/polygons for building, street, admin areas), callable from browser JS on a static GitHub Pages site without paid keys

sources.name: Nominatim (OSMF public instance) — /search, /reverse, /lookup
sources.example_request: Forward: https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/search?q=1600+Pennsylvania+Avenue+NW,+Washington,+DC&format=jsonv2&addressdetails=1&extratags=1&namedetails=1&polygon_geojson=1&limit=1   |   Reverse at the point (building level): https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/reverse?lat=38.8977&lon=-77.0365&format=jsonv2&zoom=18&addressdetails=1&extratags=1&namedetails=1&polygon_geojson=1   |   Ring ladder: repeat /reverse with zoom=17 (street), 14 (neighbourhood), 13 (suburb), 12 (town/borough), 10 (city), 8 (county), 5 (state), 3 (country) — each returns osm_type/osm_id + (with polygon_geojson=1) geometry   |   Batch polygons: https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/lookup?osm_ids=R148838,R162069&format=geojson&polygon_geojson=1&polygon_threshold=0.0005&extratags=1 (ids illustrative: USA relation 148838, DC relation 162069 — take real ids from the reverse ladder or the Overpass is_in query)
sources.what_it_gives: Free-form or structured address -> lat/lon, bbox, osm_type/osm_id, class/type, display_name, and (addressdetails=1) an address breakdown keyed by OSM-style labels: house_number, road, city_block, neighbourhood, quarter, suburb, city_district/borough, village/town/city, county, state_district, state, ISO3166-2-lvl<N>, country, country_code, sometimes continent. format=geocodejson adds a stable 'type' (house/street/district/city/county/state/country) and an 'admin' object with level2..level10 names. polygon_geojson=1 returns full geometry (building footprint, street linestring, admin multipolygon); polygon_threshold simplifies it. extratags=1 on the public server (which runs the 'extratags' import style per the OSM wiki Nominatim/FAQ) returns most other OSM tags (wikidata, wikipedia, population, building:levels, start_date where tagged); namedetails=1 returns name variants incl. old_name. /lookup takes up to 50 osm_ids per call, so one request can fetch simplified polygons for every ring. Note: name:etymology* keys are in the import's IGNORE_KEYS.name list (lib-lua/themes/nominatim/presets.lua), so they never appear in extratags — get them from Overpass.
sources.ring_or_timescale: Rings: house/lot (building way + house number), street (road + osm way id), neighbourhood/suburb/quarter/borough, city/town, county, state, country (names for all via addressdetails; osm ids + polygons via the reverse zoom ladder and /lookup). Time: present-day OSM only; occasional start_date/old_name via extratags/namedetails.
sources.license_attribution: Data © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0 — every response carries a 'licence' field with this text. Policy requires attribution 'clearly displayed as suitable for your medium': show '© OpenStreetMap contributors' linked to https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright next to the results/map.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: OSMF Nominatim Usage Policy: absolute maximum 1 request/second; provide a valid HTTP Referer or User-Agent identifying the app (a browser sends Referer automatically from your GitHub Pages origin; you cannot set User-Agent from JS — Referer satisfies the policy, so do NOT set document referrer policy to no-referrer); cache results; clearly display attribution. Unacceptable: auto-complete/search-as-you-type (explicitly forbidden client-side), systematic/bulk queries (reverse in a grid, downloading all POIs), scraping the /details endpoint (documented as 'may not be used in scripts or bots at all' — so do not use /details?hierarchy=1 for the ring tree), reselling, apps whose primary function is geocoding. Server blocks offenders with 403/429 and those error responses carry no CORS headers, so abuse shows up in the browser as a 'CORS error' (OSM dev list, Aug 2023). The reverse zoom ladder is ~8 requests, so sequence them >=1 s apart and cache per address. Non-commercial hobby use at low volume is the intended use case ('mainly there to power the search bar on openstreetmap.org').
sources.notes: CORS evidence: Nominatim's server sends access-control-allow-origin: * when NOMINATIM_CORS_NOACCESSCONTROL is on, and the documented default is 'yes' (docs/customize/Settings.md; implemented in src/nominatim_api/server/falcon/server.py and starlette/server.py). Browser libraries that call the public instance with plain fetch() — leaflet-control-geocoder (default geocoder, util.ts uses fetch with only an Accept header and enforces a 1 s client-side spacing) and leaflet-geosearch — prove it works cross-origin. Keep requests 'simple' (no custom headers like Content-Type) to avoid a preflight; a 2023 report on the OSM dev list says the server stopped sending access-control-allow-methods on GET and preflights with non-safelisted headers fail. JSONP (json_callback) also exists as a fallback. Hierarchy strategy that stays inside the policy: (1) /search once for the address with addressdetails+extratags+namedetails+polygon_geojson (gives house polygon, road name, all ring NAMES); (2) /reverse ladder at zooms 17,14,13,12,10,8,5,3 for ring osm ids (or replace this with one Overpass is_in query, see Overpass entry); (3) one /lookup with polygon_geojson=1&polygon_threshold to pull simplified polygons for all ring ids in a single request. Reverse works by nearest indexed object, so in dense areas the zoom=17/18 result may belong to a neighbouring street/building — cross-check with the search result's road/house_number. No live call was possible from this sandbox (egress proxy 403); nothing here was verified live.

votes.corrected_facts: 1. Error responses NOW carry CORS headers: since the openstreetmap/chef commit of Jun 3, 2026 ("nominatim: add CORS headers for error pages"), nginx's /403.html (for 403 and 418) and /509.html (for 429 and 503) locations send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin "*" always` plus `Vary "*"`. So a blocked/rate-limited request should surface in the browser as a real 403/429 response, not an opaque "CORS error" as the 2023 dev-list thread described. 2. Preflights with non-safelisted headers no longer fail: since Aug 2023 nginx answers OPTIONS itself with Access-Control-Allow-Origin *, Allow-Methods GET,OPTIONS and Allow-Headers echoing the requested headers (Aug 14, 2023 fix). Keeping requests "simple" is still good practice but not required. 3. The usage policy has grown clauses the claim omits: a "Usage in LLMs" section (LLMs may only suggest the service if they prominently point to the policy; LLM-generated code must comply; the public API must not be built into no-code/low-code/"vibe-coding" platforms as a generic geocoder; use is only permitted where the developer made a deliberate, informed decision and is directly responsible for compliance); "periodic requests from apps are considered bulk geocoding"; apps "must make sure that they can switch the service at our request at any time" and should "set up a proxy and also enable caching"; long-running or regularly scheduled scripts are limited to 4 requests/minute. 4. nginx-level blocking rule: a request is refused (403) when it has no email identifier, no Referer AND an empty User-Agent, or matches private UA/referrer/email blocklists; browsers normally pass. 5. Strongest evidence for the extratags import style is the chef template cookbooks/nominatim/templates/default/nominatim.env.erb (NOMINATIM_IMPORT_STYLE=extratags), not the wiki FAQ.

votes.reasoning:
Core claim stands: the OSMF Nominatim Usage Policy (source text read from the openstreetmap/owg-website repo, policies/nominatim.md, which publishes operations.osmfoundation.org/policies/nominatim/) has an explicit 'Websites and Apps' section stating that use 'directly triggered by the end-user (for example, user searches for something) is ok, provided that your number of users is moderate'. Nothing in the policy forbids browser/JavaScript use; the identification requirement is 'a valid HTTP Referer or User-Agent', and a browser's automatic Referer (origin of the GitHub Pages site) satisfies it. CORS is confirmed by Nominatim's NOMINATIM_CORS_NOACCESSCONTROL default (yes) and by the OSMF nginx template, which also answers OPTIONS preflights with Access-Control-Allow-Origin '*'. Attribution and ODbL obligations are as the claim states. /details is forbidden for scripts (docs/api/Details.md warning + policy 'Scraping of details'). /lookup accepts up to 50 ids. So a small hobby site calling /search, /reverse and /lookup from visitors' browsers at low volume, with Referer, attribution and caching, is within policy and would not normally be blocked.

However the claim misstates or omits several policy and sustainability points that matter for this design:
1. The 1 request/second limit is per website/application — 'the sum of traffic by all your users should not exceed the limits' — not per visitor. A purely client-side 1 s spacing only bounds one browser; it cannot enforce the site-wide limit. With the claim's ~10 Nominatim calls per address (1 search + 8-step reverse zoom ladder + 1 lookup), one lookup consumes the whole site's quota for ~10 s, and two concurrent visitors would already exceed the policy limit. Tolerable for a few users, but the ladder should be replaced (one /reverse with addressdetails for names, Overpass is_in or one /lookup for ids/polygons) to keep Nominatim calls at 1-2 per address.
2. The policy says 'If at all possible, set up a proxy and also enable caching of requests' and 'Apps must make sure that they can switch the service at our request at any time'. The direct-from-browser, no-proxy design is permitted but runs against the stated preference; per-browser localStorage caching cannot dedupe identical queries across visitors ('Clients sending repeatedly the same query may be classified as faulty and blocked'). A static site should at least keep the endpoint configurable so it can be switched by redeploy.
3. Blocking is site-wide: the OSMF nginx config blocks by Referer list (nginx_blocked_referrer.conf) as well as by IP/User-Agent/email, so one abusive pattern blocks every visitor of the site at once. 403.html says blocks usually lift after hours of inactivity; 429 ('Bandwidth limit exceeded') blocks lift automatically.
4. Enforcement history shows reverse is treated as costly: from Dec 2024 (commit feac058 'clamp down on rate limits': www zone 2r/s -> 1r/s) until Mar 2026, nginx enforced 1 r/s (burst 10, status 429) plus a separate 10 requests/minute limit on /reverse; an 8-step reverse ladder per address would have tripped that. On 2026-03-06 (0e9bffe) all nginx rate limiting was removed because it interfered with Fastly caching (Fastly fronting since Nov 2025); enforcement is now at the edge/manual (a 2026 community thread reports 429s lasting ~5 minutes with Retry-After: 0), so exact current thresholds are not public.
5. The claim's note that 403/429 responses carry no CORS headers (so abuse appears as a 'CORS error') is outdated: commit 0b701b6 (2026-06-03, 'nominatim: add CORS headers for error pages') added Access-Control-Allow-Origin '*' always to the 403 and 429/503 pages, so blocks now surface as real HTTP 403/429 in the browser.
6. The policy now has a 'Usage in LLMs' section: LLM-generated code must adhere to all terms, and use is permitted only where the developer 'has made a deliberate, informed decision to use it and is directly responsible for complying'. Since this plan is LLM-researched, the site owner must consciously accept the policy.
7. 'Reselling of geocoding results: Applications and services whose primary function is related to geocoding must run their own service.' A place-history site is not primarily a geocoder, so this is likely fine, but it is a judgement call the owner should make.
8. Sustainability: the policy says the service 'runs on donated servers and has a very limited capacity', 'may change without notice' and 'you might have your access withdrawn'; the public pool is 8 gunicorn workers (api_pool_size 10, 5 s query timeout) with a separate 2-worker 'fastlane' reserved for openstreetmap.org's own frontends. Fine for a hobby site, but a fallback (own instance or a provider) should be planned.
9. Minor: the 1 s client-side spacing in leaflet-control-geocoder lives in src/geocoders/nominatim.ts (MIN_REQUEST_INTERVAL = 1000, _rateLimit()), not in util.ts, which only wraps fetch with an Accept header.

Limitations: operations.osmfoundation.org, community/help/lists/wiki.openstreetmap.org, nominatim.org and git.openstreetmap.org were egress-blocked, so the policy text comes from its GitHub source repo and the community threads only from search snippets; GitHub commit diffs were read via github.com HTML pages. No live request was possible.
votes.corrected_facts: (a) The 1 req/s maximum applies per website/application (sum of all visitors), not per visitor; client-side spacing does not satisfy it. (b) The policy asks sites to set up a proxy and caching 'if at all possible' and to be able to switch the service at OSMF's request; it also contains a 'Usage in LLMs' clause requiring a deliberate, informed decision by the developer. (c) Since 2026-06-03 the OSMF nginx config sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on 403/429/503 error pages, so blocks appear as HTTP 403/429, not as CORS errors; the Aug-2023 dev-list statement is obsolete. (d) nginx enforced 1 r/s plus a 10 req/min limit specifically on /reverse from Dec 2024 to Mar 2026; all nginx rate limiting was removed on 2026-03-06 (Fastly in front since Nov 2025), so current edge thresholds are not public and reverse-heavy patterns (an 8-step zoom ladder per address) are a risk — prefer 1-2 Nominatim calls per address. (e) Blocking is by Referer/IP/User-Agent/email lists, so a block hits the whole site. (f) leaflet-control-geocoder's 1 s spacing is in src/geocoders/nominatim.ts, not util.ts.

sources.name: Overpass API — overpass-api.de (main) with overpass.private.coffee / overpass.kumi.systems and maps.mail.ru as fallbacks
sources.what_it_gives: Raw OSM objects around/containing a point with ALL their tags and (optionally) geometry: the building footprint way/relation, the street way(s), and the nested admin boundary relations found via is_in + pivot. Unlike Nominatim it returns start_date, historic=*, heritage, old_name, name:etymology / name:etymology:wikidata, building:levels, etc. Admin polygon geometry is available with 'out geom' but is very large for state/country relations — prefer 'out tags bb' (bbox only) for those and get simplified polygons from Nominatim /lookup, or self-simplify in the browser.
sources.ring_or_timescale: Rings: house/lot (building footprint + address node), block (ring of surrounding named streets), street (highway way ids/geometry), neighbourhood only where mapped as an area (place=* relation/closed way; many neighbourhoods are nodes and will not be found by is_in), city/county/state/country (boundary=administrative relations with admin_level 2..10, incl. ids and wikidata). Time: present day; tags start_date / old_name / historic / name:etymology give sparse point-in-time hints.
sources.license_attribution: Data © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0 — show '© OpenStreetMap contributors' linked to https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright (overpass-turbo's own config quotes the OSMF attribution guideline: attribution must be to 'OpenStreetMap' and make the ODbL clear). Overpass server software is AGPL but that does not affect API consumers.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: overpass-api.de (Commons page / OSM wiki): you can assume you don't disturb other users at <10,000 queries/day and <1 GB download/day, and these numbers count for your app in aggregate across all its users; add a User-Agent or Referer that identifies your app (browser Referer suffices); expect HTTP 429 (per-IP slot limit, typically 2 concurrent slots, visible at https://overpass-api.de/api/status) and 504 under load; wiki says commercial use should self-host or pay; the main server has been blocking whole cloud IP ranges during abuse waves (2025 forum thread), so build retry/failover. overpass.private.coffee (same operator as overpass.kumi.systems, which still answers): wiki entry says 'feel free to use in any project, there is no rate limit in place', notify them for large-scale projects; planet-wide data. maps.mail.ru/osm/tools/overpass/api/interpreter: planet-wide public mirror listed on the wiki and in overpass-turbo's fallback list. Keep [timeout:25] and small 'around' radii; one combined query per address keeps you far under the limits.
sources.notes: CORS is baked into the server: web_output.cc prints 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *', 'Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS' and Access-Control-Allow-Headers for every response, so any instance running stock Overpass answers browser requests. overpass-turbo itself is a static site that does fetch(`${server}interpreter`, {method:'POST', body: URLSearchParams({data: query})}) straight from the browser to overpass-api.de (js/overpass.ts), and its configs.ts lists overpass-api.de, maps.mail.ru and overpass.private.coffee as suggested servers (it also reads the live instance table from the wiki). Third-party browser code using the exact is_in/pivot pattern for the admin ring: metro-dreamin (Next.js page: `is_in(lat,lng)->.a;rel(pivot.a)[boundary=administrative];out tags;` plus `way[highway][name](around:500,...)`), osmapa (searchService.js), Tabi (js/api.js: `is_in(lat,lng)->.a; area.a[admin_level=8][boundary=administrative]->.b; rel(pivot.b); out geom;`). Use a POST with a URL-encoded body (no custom headers) so the request is a CORS 'simple request' — no preflight. Tag availability is sparse: start_date is on well under 1% of buildings; name:etymology:wikidata exists mainly where etymology-mapping projects were active; always treat these as bonuses, not the primary history source. Data is minutes behind live OSM. Not verified live from this sandbox.

votes.reasoning: PRIMARY ENDPOINT CONFIRMED. (2) CORS: drolbr/Overpass-API master src/overpass_api/frontend/web_output.cc lines 136-147 and 163-174 print "Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *" and "Access-Control-Max-Age: 600" whenever the request carried an Origin header (`if (has_origin)`), echo Access-Control-Allow-Headers when supplied, and print "Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS" on OPTIONS. So the claim's "for every response" is slightly inaccurate (conditional on Origin; methods only on preflight) but browsers always send Origin cross-origin, so functionally correct. Third-party browser code confirms it works: metro-dreamin pages/edit/[systemId].js lines 1003-1026 (fetch POST to overpass-api.de with `is_in(lat,lng)->.a;rel(pivot.a)[boundary=administrative];out tags;`) and osmapa js/search/searchService.js line 118 (is_in/pivot via $http POST to //overpass-api.de/api/interpreter). PARTS OF THE CLAIM THAT ARE WRONG OR OUTDATED (as of 2026-10-07): (A) "overpass.kumi.systems, which still answers" is false: it is only the former hostname of private.coffee (wiki: "previously known as overpass.kumi.systems") and it timed out in every recent probe: shohei0205/yamamuki PR #37 (2026-09-29 18:38 JST: no response in 40 s), CodingDutchie/comebacktowns PR #25 (early Oct 2026 from Cloudflare edge: timeout), knoxmap PR #17 (2026-10-05: "kumi.systems was not answering at all"), marola-site #63 (2026-10-06: timeouts). The OSM wiki status page says "Coffee works, but no longer updates its database" and in another entry "The two Russian servers & 'coffee' are shut down". The wiki table's "no rate limit" text still exists but describes a non-working instance. (C) maps.mail.ru does answer server-side with fresh data (track-your-regions 2026-09-29: 200 in 0.3 s, data 2026-09-28T22:55Z; osm-mcp 2026-10-02: 200 in 15-22 s x3; comebacktowns early Oct 2026 from Cloudflare: 200 in 13 s; knoxmap 2026-10-05 adds it "as a data-returning server"), but browser CORS for it is UNVERIFIED and has a counter-report: tyrasd/overpass-turbo issue #835 (2026-04-06) reports that selecting maps.mail.ru in the browser IDE yields "Request rejected ... Error-Code: Forbidden (403)" (reporter says other Russian-based servers behaved the same; closed without comment). No source shows an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header from mail.ru; zbycz/osmapp lists it as a last-resort host in browser code but that is an assumption, not a test. (D) overpass-api.de access caveats the claim omits: the Apache front end returns 406 Not Acceptable (with no CORS headers) when the request lacks a User-Agent, and over TLS requires a Referer plus a browser-like UA (community thread "Overpass API - Error 406", t/143198); ha-bosch-ebike v1.8.4 release notes (2026-04-29) report that browser requests from private-LAN origins get HTTP 406 with no Access-Control-Allow-Origin regardless of GET/POST, so localhost/intranet dev origins may fail where a public https site works. The server has had chronic 504s through 2026 (forum thread "Overpass API performance issues" since ~Feb 2026; probes 2026-09-29: 504 in 9 s; 2026-10-02: 504, 504, no answer; PR #48: "200 most of the time but 504 when busy"); from a Cloudflare Worker it returned 521/timeout, consistent with cloud-range blocking (thread "Overpass API will block Azure and AWS for some time", t/136817). A new quota regime is in force: usage per IP and per app is metered within a 24 h window (~10 minutes CPU per day) and exceeding it yields a hard ban until the quota refills; ~15k IPs banned via quota plus ~15k via permanently banned apps (wiki status page / forum). (E) Minor misattribution: the Commons page contains no User-Agent/Referer advice and no "aggregate across your app's users" statement; those come from the forum/Apache rules and the wiki, not Commons. VERDICT: the core claim (endpoint exists at that URL with those parameters, callable from browser JS via stock CORS headers, no key) is supported by source code and multiple independent browser clients, so not refuted; but two of the three listed fallbacks are dead/stale, the third's browser CORS is unproven with a 403 report, and the access conditions on the main server are stricter than described. Then fetch simplified ring polygons in a single Nominatim /lookup?osm_ids=R..,R..&polygon_geojson=1&polygon_threshold=... call rather than pulling state/country geometry through Overpass. domain: Wikipedia / Wikidata / Wikimedia Commons as sources of written history and dated historical images for the address-rings site (street, neighborhood, city, county, state, country, plus individual notable buildings)

sources.name: Wikipedia Action API (geosearch + extracts + parse + pageprops) on en.wikipedia.org
sources.example_request:
Nearby articles with coords, QIDs, intro text and thumbnails in ONE call:
https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&format=json&formatversion=2&origin=*&generator=geosearch&ggscoord=38.8977|-77.0365&ggsradius=1000&ggslimit=50&ggsprimary=all&prop=coordinates|pageprops|pageimages|extracts&coprop=type|dim|name&ppprop=wikibase_item&piprop=thumbnail&pithumbsize=320&exintro=1&explaintext=1&exlimit=20

History section of a ring article (2 calls): (1) https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=parse&format=json&formatversion=2&origin=*&page=Washington,_D.C.&prop=sections  -> find the section whose line == "History" (toclevel 1) and read its index N; (2) https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=parse&format=json&formatversion=2&origin=*&page=Washington,_D.C.&section=N&prop=text|wikitext&disabletoc=1&disableeditsection=1

Whole 'History of <City>' article as plain text with == headings == (one page per call): https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&format=json&formatversion=2&origin=*&prop=extracts&explaintext=1&exsectionformat=wiki&redirects=1&titles=History_of_Washington,_D.C.

Probe whether 'History of X' / 'Timeline of X' exist: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&format=json&formatversion=2&origin=*&redirects=1&prop=info|pageprops&ppprop=wikibase_item&titles=History_of_Washington,_D.C.|Timeline_of_Washington,_D.C.  (pages with "missing":true do not exist)
sources.what_it_gives: list=geosearch / generator=geosearch returns every article with coordinates within 10-10000 m of a point (max 500 results), with distance, and with coprop=type a GeoData category (city, landmark, edu, railwaystation, etc.) that is handy for deciding which ring a hit belongs to. Combining it with prop=pageprops (ppprop=wikibase_item) gives the Wikidata QID for every hit, prop=extracts gives intro text (exintro, max 20 pages per call; full-article extracts are 1 page per call), prop=pageimages gives a lead thumbnail. action=parse&prop=sections lists section titles/indexes so you can fetch exactly the 'History' section as HTML or wikitext; the section HTML contains the {{Main|History of X}} hatnote (div.hatnote a[href]) which is the cheapest way to discover the dedicated 'History of <City>' article; otherwise use Wikidata P2184 ('history of topic', e.g. Argentina -> History of Argentina) or a title probe with redirects=1. Also list=search (srsearch) for 'History of <neighborhood>' style lookups.
sources.ring_or_timescale: Rings: house/lot (NRHP-listed and other notable buildings within ~100-300 m), street (articles exist for major/named streets; use gsprop/coprop type=landmark and title matching), neighborhood, city/town, county, state, country (each has a page whose History section and 'History of X' article give the narrative). Time scales: written history, i.e. years -> decades -> centuries; city/country articles reach back millennia (founding, pre-colonial, archaeology); no per-point deep time (only 'Geology of <state/region>' articles).
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: CORS mechanism confirmed from MediaWiki source: ApiMain::handleCORS() treats origin=* as an anonymous cross-origin request and emits 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' (plus 'Access-Control-Allow-Methods: POST, GET, HEAD' on preflight); preflighted custom headers are allowed only if in $wgAllowedCorsHeaders, whose default list includes 'User-Agent' and 'Api-User-Agent' (MainConfigSchema.php). Browser-side open-source callers: tomayac/wikipedia-around (fetch to en.wikipedia.org ...list=geosearch...&origin=* then prop=extracts&exintro&explaintext) and tbo47/ez-opendata (same, plus Commons). Limits from source + WMF config: gsradius 10..10000 m (wgMaxGeoSearchRadius default 10000 in InitialiseSettings.php), gslimit max 500, exlimit max 20 and only with exintro (ApiQueryExtracts forces limit=1 otherwise), exchars max 1200, exsentences max 10. Rate limits (new, 2026, 'subject to experimentation and change'): WMF global per-user limits apply across all sites to Action and REST APIs; requests made from a web browser by an unauthenticated user get 200 requests/min; 'unidentified' non-browser requests (IP only, no contact info in UA) get 10 requests/min; stricter limits on unidentified/browser traffic from early March 2026, identified traffic re-tiered in April 2026; 429 + Retry-After must be honored. Legacy etiquette still applies: send requests serially, batch titles (up to 50 per call), use formatversion=2 and redirects=1. User-Agent policy: a browser cannot set User-Agent, so the policy's workaround is the Api-User-Agent header; it is CORS-whitelisted on the Action API (costs one cached preflight, see Access-Control-Max-Age in the whitelist). Could not fetch the policy pages themselves here (egress block); numbers come from search snippets of mediawiki.org/wiki/Wikimedia_APIs/Rate_limits and the Wikitech-l 'New global API rate limits' thread.
sources.license_attribution: Article text is CC BY-SA 4.0 for edits since the June 2023 Terms of Use change (older revisions CC BY-SA 3.0, which 4.0 reuse is compatible with). For each snippet shown: name the article, link to it, state 'CC BY-SA 4.0' with a link to the license; derived/edited text must stay share-alike. Thumbnails from pageimages are Commons files with their own per-file license (see Commons source).
sources.notes: Practical pattern for the rings: geocode first (outside this domain) to get the lat/lon and the admin names; then one generator=geosearch call for the house/street/neighborhood rings (filter by coprop type and dist), and one prop=pageprops|extracts call with titles=<City>|<County>|<State>|<Country> for the outer rings. Section extraction: Parsoid/REST HTML (next source) is cleaner than action=parse for programmatic section slicing, but action=parse&section=N gives wikitext, from which you can regex the {{Main|History of X}} hatnote. Evidence copies of the sources I grepped are saved under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-sno-ball/a6069c2d-56e0-5914-9c8c-c420aa5c5797/scratchpad/gh/ (ApiMain.php, MainConfigSchema.php, ApiQueryGeoSearch.php, TextExtracts.php, ApiParse.php, InitialiseSettings.php, wikipedia-around.js, ez-opendata.ts).

votes.corrected_facts:
1. "Nearby articles with coords, QIDs, intro text and thumbnails in ONE call" with ggslimit=50 is only partly true: prop=coordinates has a default colimit of 10 (QueryCoordinates.php), so the first response carries coordinates for just 10 of the 50 pages plus a `continue` block; add `colimit=50` (max 500). prop=extracts is hard-capped at 20 pages per call (exlimit max 20), so with 50 generator hits you must either set ggslimit=20 or follow `continue`/`excontinue`. pilimit defaults to 50, so pageimages is fine.
2. generator=geosearch does not return `dist`: in QueryGeoSearchDb/Elastic the dist field is only emitted when the module runs as list=geosearch ($resultPageSet === null). To get distances in the generator form, add `codistancefrompoint=38.8977|-77.0365` to the prop=coordinates request (or use list=geosearch).
3. action=parse&prop=sections is deprecated since MediaWiki 1.46 (T319141); the replacement is prop=tocdata. It still works on en.wikipedia.org (which runs weekly master builds, now 1.47-wmf.x) but adds a deprecation warning; prefer prop=tocdata.
4. Exposed headers include Retry-After, so a browser client can read the 429 back-off. Sending Api-User-Agent (or any non-simple header) triggers one preflight; it is in the default $wgAllowedCorsHeaders so it succeeds.
5. Rate limits (2026 pages, via search snippets): unauthenticated browser requests 200 req/min; unidentified non-browser requests 10 req/min; identified (compliant User-Agent with contact) 200 req/min; Toolforge/WMCS and bot-flagged accounts exempt; Phase 1 enforcement March 2026, Phase 2 April 2026, rollout reported complete later in 2026. 6. The saved evidence copy "ApiQueryGeoSearch.php" corresponds to the current file includes/Api/QueryGeoSearch.php (class GeoData\Api\QueryGeoSearch); the extracts module file is includes/ApiQueryExtracts.php.

sources.name: Wikipedia REST API / Page Content Service (page summary, Parsoid HTML, media-list)
sources.example_request:
Card for the nearest hit (title comes from geosearch): https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/summary/White_House  -> JSON with extract, extract_html, description, thumbnail{source,width,height}, originalimage, coordinates{lat:38.8977,lon:-77.0365}, wikibase_item (QID), content_urls, timestamp

Full article as sectioned Parsoid HTML (slice the History section client-side): https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Washington,_D.C.  -> look for <section data-mw-section-id="N"><h2 id="History">...; the hatnote inside links to History_of_Washington,_D.C.

Images used in a ring article (captions + Commons titles, good for 'historical photo of this city' without geosearch): https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/media-list/History_of_Washington,_D.C.

Fallback for HTML served by MediaWiki core REST: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/rest.php/v1/page/White_House/html
sources.what_it_gives: page/summary: a cached, tiny JSON card per article (plain-text and HTML intro, lead image, page coordinates, Wikidata QID, short description) - the cheapest way to render a ring card. page/html and page/mobile-html: the whole article as Parsoid HTML with <section data-mw-section-id> wrappers and stable heading ids, which makes 'give me just the History section' a DOMParser one-liner and keeps hatnotes/infobox/images. page/media-list: every image/video in an article with captions and Commons file titles (feed those titles to Commons imageinfo to get dates/licenses). page/mobile-sections was decommissioned in July 2023; do not design around it. No geosearch in this API - pair it with Action API geosearch or Wikidata.
sources.ring_or_timescale: All rings once you know an article title (building, street, neighborhood, city, county, state, country). Time: same as Wikipedia text (years to millennia); 'History of <City>' and 'Timeline of <City>' articles are often decade-by-decade and are the best match for the time slider's historical range.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: CORS confirmed from the service source: mediawiki-services-mobileapps app.js defaults app.conf.cors to '*' and sets 'access-control-allow-origin: *' on every response, with 'access-control-allow-headers: accept, x-requested-with, content-type' and exposes etag; config.dev.yaml ships cors: "*". For the MediaWiki-core REST fallback (/w/rest.php/v1/...), CorsUtils::modifyResponse emits 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' when $wgAllowCrossOrigin is true, and Wikimedia production sets 'wgAllowCrossOrigin' => ['default' => true] (InitialiseSettings.php line ~856). PCS summary.js shows the summary fields incl. wikibase_item (from pageprops) and coordinates (from meta.geo). Important CORS caveat: the PCS allow-headers list does NOT include Api-User-Agent or User-Agent, so sending a custom header to /api/rest_v1 from a browser fails the preflight - send plain GETs with no custom headers (the WMF docs also note the REST APIs do not accept Api-User-Agent). Rate policy: REST docs ask clients to stay under 200 requests/s overall, with some endpoints stricter; the 2026 global per-user limits (200 req/min for browser traffic) apply to REST as well; responses are edge-cached so summary calls are cheap for the infrastructure. page/related is deprecated; page/mobile-sections removed July 2023 (use page/mobile-html or page/html).
sources.license_attribution: Same as Wikipedia text: CC BY-SA 4.0 (3.0 for pre-2023 revisions); content_urls in the summary gives the canonical link to attribute. Images referenced are Commons files with per-file licenses.
sources.notes: Summary extract is the lead only; for the History narrative fetch page/html and slice by data-mw-section-id, or request the Action API parse endpoint. Parsoid HTML has absolute //upload.wikimedia.org image URLs and ./relative article links - rewrite hrefs before rendering. Titles must be URL-encoded with underscores (encodeURIComponent on 'Washington,_D.C.').

votes.reasoning: Live calls to en.wikipedia.org are blocked by the sandbox proxy (403 CONNECT), so verification is from Wikimedia's production configuration and service source on GitHub mirrors. EXISTENCE: the production REST gateway values (wikimedia/operations-deployment-charts, helmfile.d/services/rest-gateway/values.yaml) define routes ma_summary_no_revision ('/+([^/]+)/v1/page/summary/(.+)'), ma_media_list_no_revision ('/+([^/]+)/v1/page/media-list/(.+)') and ma_mobile_no_revision to the mobileapps (PCS) cluster, and page-html-title ('/+([^/]+)/v1/page/html/(.+)' -> '/w/rest.php/v1/page/\2/html') to MediaWiki core (T374683). PCS master has routes/page/summary.js (router.get('/summary/:title/:revision?/:tid?')) and routes/page/media.js (router.get('/media-list/:title/:revision?/:tid?')); routes/page/related.js and mobile-sections.js return 404 (removed, consistent with the claim). lib/summary.js still emits wikibase_item (meta.pageprops), coordinates (meta.geo), extract_html, originalimage, content_urls, timestamp. CORS: routes with rb_response_headers: true (all the PCS routes and the page/html compat route) make Envoy OVERWRITE_IF_EXISTS_OR_ADD 'access-control-allow-origin: *', 'access-control-allow-methods: GET,HEAD', 'access-control-allow-headers: accept, content-type, content-length, cache-control, accept-language, api-user-agent, if-match, if-modified-since, if-none-match, dnt, accept-encoding', 'access-control-expose-headers: etag' (charts/api-gateway/templates/_rest_routes.yaml lines 133-149); helmfile.d/services/rest-gateway/tests/test_cors.py asserts exactly these headers on rb-compat routes. The /w/rest.php/v1/page/{title}/html fallback is routed via the 'mw-rest-php' block which defers to MediaWiki headers; CorsUtils::modifyResponse sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * for anonymous requests when AllowCrossOrigin is true, and production InitialiseSettings.php line 856 sets 'wgAllowCrossOrigin' => ['default' => true]; MainConfigSchema default AllowedCorsHeaders includes Api-User-Agent and User-Agent for preflights. API KEY: none. The gateway lua (charts/api-gateway/lua/restgw_ratelimits.lua) classifies unauthenticated requests as anon-browser (x-is-browser score >= 35), unauthed-bot (x-ua-contact present), or anon; the production 'May2026' policy (shadow_mode: false, i.e. enforced) gives anon-browser 200/min, unauthed-bot 200/min, anon 10/min, authed-user 200/min, established-user 2000/min; OPTIONS requests are exempt (T418969). JWT auth is optional and only raises limits. This matches the mediawiki.org Rate_limits page (200/min for browser and compliant-UA traffic, 10/min for IP-only) and the March 2026 wikitech-l 'New global API rate limits' rollout. Nothing found indicating the rest_v1 page/summary, page/html or page/media-list paths have been or are scheduled to be removed; T374683 says callers 'will eventually be moved to new canonical urls' but none are defined yet. Minor inaccuracies exist (see corrected_facts) but the core existence/CORS/no-key claim stands.
votes.corrected_facts: 1) The CORS caveat in the claim is outdated: on /api/rest_v1 the REST gateway overwrites PCS's own CORS headers, and its access-control-allow-headers list DOES include api-user-agent (plus accept-language, cache-control, if-none-match, etc.). The mobileapps app.js list ('accept, x-requested-with, content-type') never reaches the browser. Sending Api-User-Agent from browser JS should pass preflight (OPTIONS is also exempt from rate limiting). Plain GETs remain the simplest option. 2) https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/ no longer serves swagger docs; it 301-redirects to Special:RestSandbox/wmf-rest (T396807). The JSON spec is at /api/rest_v1/?spec -> /api/restbase_specs/rest_v1-wikipedia.json. 3) /api/rest_v1/page/html/{title} is no longer RESTBase/Parsoid storage; it is a gateway rewrite to MediaWiki core /w/rest.php/v1/page/{title}/html (T374683), so the 'fallback' and primary are the same backend. T374683 says these rest_v1 paths will eventually move to new canonical URLs, but none are defined yet (expected to take months or longer). 4) The old 'stay under 200 requests/s' REST guidance is superseded by the 2026 gateway limits: anon-browser 200/min, compliant-User-Agent bot 200/min, unidentified IP-only 10/min, authenticated 200/min, established editors 2000/min (production May2026 policy, enforced, not shadow). Browser classification depends on the CDN's x-is-browser score (production threshold 35); a cross-origin fetch() from a real browser should qualify, but a server-side or headless client without a contact-info User-Agent falls to 10/min per IP. 5) The /page/summary api_urls field is slated for removal (announced on mediawiki-api-announce); other summary fields are unaffected. 6) wgRestAllowCrossOriginCookieAuth is false by default in production (true only on metawiki), which is irrelevant for anonymous requests (they still get '*').

sources.name: Wikidata Query Service (SPARQL endpoint, query.wikidata.org)
sources.what_it_gives: Structured facts for every ring and for notable buildings: wikibase:around radius search on P625 (radius in km; wikibase:distance binds km), P131 'located in the administrative territorial entity' chains (wdt:P131+ for the current chain; p:P131 statements with pq:P580/pq:P582 for historical membership), P571 inception / P576 dissolved, P1082 population with pq:P585 point-in-time (census-year series for most cities and countries), P138 named after (streets, neighborhoods, buildings), P649 NRHP reference number, P1435 heritage designation, P84 architect, P149 architectural style, P1619 opening date, P6 head of government with P580/P582 (mayor/governor by year), P793 significant event with P585, P2184 'history of topic' (links a place to its 'History of X' item), P1366/P1365 and P155/P156 for predecessor/successor polities (which country/colony was this in year X), P30 continent, P373 Commons category, P18 image, and sitelinks (schema:about / schema:isPartOf <https://en.wikipedia.org/>) to jump to Wikipedia titles.
sources.ring_or_timescale: Rings: house (NRHP/heritage buildings with P625; coverage is dense in the US thanks to NRHP imports), street (only notable streets have items; P625 on streets is sparse), neighborhood, city, county, state, country, continent (P30). Time: year-by-year (population P585 series, office-holders, significant events) through decades/centuries (inception/dissolution of polities, historical-country items with P571/P576); nothing geological.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: CORS: the endpoint is CORS-enabled (Leskoff 'How to query Wikidata using SPARQL in JavaScript': 'supports CORS, allowing you to send queries directly from the client'; wikibase-sdk docs target browsers and build fetch URLs to https://query.wikidata.org/sparql?format=json&query=...). Browser-side open-source proof: johnsamuelwrites/wdprop (a static GitHub Pages site) does fetch('https://query.wikidata.org/sparql?query=...&format=json') from the page; tbo47/ez-opendata fetches https://query.wikidata.org/bigdata/namespace/wdq/sparql?format=json&query= from the browser. Phabricator T308180 (local Blazegraph lacks the CORS header that production WDQS has) corroborates. Caveat (T362570, 'Allow CORS with (Api-)User-Agent header to query.wikidata.org'): the WDQS preflight does not list User-Agent/Api-User-Agent in Access-Control-Allow-Headers, so adding those headers from a browser makes the request fail - send a plain GET with ?format=json (or Accept: application/sparql-results+json, a safelisted header) and no custom headers. Limits (WDQS user manual / query limits page): hard query timeout 60 s; 5 parallel queries per IP; one client (UA+IP) gets 60 s of processing per 60 s and 30 error queries per minute; excess returns 429 with Retry-After, and ignoring 429 can get the client temporarily banned; limits 'subject to change'. Design: at most 1-2 small queries per address, always LIMIT, prefer wdt: (truthy) paths, keep radius small (0.3-2 km), cache by QID. Fallback engine: QLever's Wikidata endpoint (https://qlever.cs.uni-freiburg.de/api/wikidata) is listed by wikibase-sdk as an alternative - CORS not verified here.
sources.license_attribution: Wikidata content is CC0 1.0 (no attribution legally required; WMF asks that you make the CC0 terms clear and a 'Data from Wikidata' link is good practice).
sources.notes: Use the around query for the inner rings and the P131 chain for the outer rings; the P131 chain also yields the QIDs you then feed to Wikipedia (via sitelinks) and Commons (via P373 category / depicts). P131 is not strictly a tree (dual memberships, historical entities) - take the chain members whose P31 is a settlement/county/state/country class and dedupe. Historical P131/P17 qualifiers (P580/P582) are sparse outside Europe, so do not rely on them for the time slider; use P571/P576 of polities plus predecessor links instead.

votes.reasoning:
Core claim (endpoint exists at https://query.wikidata.org/sparql, GET ?format=json&query= or form-POST, CORS-enabled for any origin, no API key) is CONFIRMED from the production infrastructure source, not just blog posts. I could not reach query.wikidata.org, wikidata.org, mediawiki.org, meta, wikitech, phabricator, lists, diff or mail-archive from the sandbox (egress 403), so live verification was impossible; the web-search budget was exhausted near the end.

EXISTENCE: wikimedia/operations-puppet (branch production) modules/query_service/templates/nginx.erb contains `rewrite ^/sparql$ /bigdata/namespace/<%= @blazegraph_main_ns %>/sparql;` and hieradata/role/common/wdqs/main.yaml sets `profile::query_service::blazegraph_main_ns: wdq`, so /sparql and /bigdata/namespace/wdq/sparql are the same endpoint. The SPARQL location allows `limit_except GET OPTIONS POST`, default 60 s max query time (`max_query_time_millis` default 60000), `limit_conn byaddr 5` with `limit_conn_status 429`. The file was last touched Sep 8 2026 (commit list), and the Feb 2026 removal was of the LDF endpoint only. hieradata/role/common/cache/text.yaml still lists query.wikidata.org (plus new query-next.wikidata.org / query-scholarly-next.wikidata.org hosts). Graph split (May 2025) means query.wikidata.org serves the main graph; places/admin entities are unaffected.

CORS: in nginx.erb the SPARQL location has, for the non-OAuth case, `add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin * always;` and `add_header Access-Control-Allow-Headers "accept, content-type, content-length, user-agent, api-user-agent";`. wdqs/main.yaml and wdqs/scholarly.yaml set `profile::query_service::oauth: false` (only wcqs/public.yaml, the Commons service, sets true), so the wildcard branch is the one deployed for query.wikidata.org. Browser consumers confirmed in source: johnsamuelwrites/wdprop wdprop.js (DOM-manipulating page) does fetch('https://query.wikidata.org/sparql?query=...&format=json', {headers:{Accept:'application/sparql-results+json'}}); tbo47/ez-opendata index.ts (browser-targeted) fetches https://query.wikidata.org/bigdata/namespace/wdq/sparql?format=json&query=.

NO API KEY: no auth_request/OAuth on the WDQS SPARQL location (oauth=false); the only identity rule is nginx `return 403` for an empty User-Agent and Blazegraph's RealAgentFilter/ThrottlingFilter (web.xml) keyed on UA+IP; browsers always send a UA.

Corrections found: (1) the claim's caveat about T362570 is stale – commit a68c3e535ebde7aec6c18b94bd82e6eb477e2e5b (Jun 27 2024, 'Bug: T362570') added user-agent and api-user-agent to Access-Control-Allow-Headers, so Api-User-Agent from a browser now passes preflight. (2) wikibase-sdk's QLever alternative is now https://qlever.dev/wikidata (API https://qlever.dev/api/wikidata), not qlever.cs.uni-freiburg.de. (3) The endpoint is on a published sunset path: WMF/WMDE chose QLever as the WDQS v2 backend with new endpoint URLs (query-next.wikidata.org appears in CDN config); per the wikidata.org 'WDQS backend update' page (seen only via search summaries) the Blazegraph endpoint may degrade from Feb 2027 and is to be decommissioned by June 30 2027. The claim's queries rely on Blazegraph-only services (SERVICE wikibase:around, SERVICE wikibase:label); QLever has no native wikibase:label (ad-freiburg/qlever#1829 open) and no wikibase:around, so they will need rewriting for v2. (4) Rate limits: besides WDQS's own limits, WMF rolled out global API rate limits in Mar/Apr 2026 (Tech News 2026/10; mediawiki.org Wikimedia_APIs/Rate_limits – search-only). The Varnish misc-frontend VCL that serves query.wikidata.org applies UA-policy throttling (e.g. python-requests UA: 10 req/10 s) and etcd-driven requestctl filters to unidentified/browser traffic whose values are not in the repo, so exact browser-origin limits are unverified; at 1–2 queries per address this is immaterial. Note nginx-generated 429s from limit_conn (location @rate_limit) do not carry the CORS header in non-OAuth mode, so a browser sees them as a fetch TypeError rather than a readable 429; Blazegraph-generated 429s (with Retry-After) pass through the location and do get the CORS header.
votes.corrected_facts: 1) T362570 caveat is outdated: since 2024-06-27 (operations-puppet commit a68c3e5, Bug: T362570) query.wikidata.org's SPARQL responses include Access-Control-Allow-Headers "accept, content-type, content-length, user-agent, api-user-agent", so sending Api-User-Agent (or User-Agent) from browser JS no longer fails preflight; it merely triggers an OPTIONS preflight. sources.name: Wikidata entity API (Special:EntityData JSON + wbgetentities / wbsearchentities on www.wikidata.org)
sources.example_request:
Batch fetch the ring items once their QIDs are known (White House Q35525, Washington D.C. Q61, United States Q30, North America Q49):
https://www.wikidata.org/w/api.php?action=wbgetentities&ids=Q35525|Q61|Q30|Q49&props=labels|descriptions|claims|sitelinks&languages=en&sitefilter=enwiki|commonswiki&format=json&formatversion=2&origin=*

Single entity, linked-data style (also CORS-enabled, strongly cached):
https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Special:EntityData/Q35525.json

Name lookup for a street or neighborhood typed by the user:
https://www.wikidata.org/w/api.php?action=wbsearchentities&search=Pennsylvania%20Avenue&language=en&type=item&limit=10&format=json&origin=*
sources.what_it_gives: The full claim set of an item as JSON (every statement with qualifiers and references), so without SPARQL you can read P131 (with P580/P582 qualifiers), P571/P576, P1082 population statements each carrying its pq P585 date, P138, P649, P1435, P625, P18 image, P373 Commons category, P2184 history-of-topic item, plus labels/descriptions and sitelinks (enwiki title for the Wikipedia calls, commonswiki for the category). wbsearchentities gives fuzzy label search for user-typed names. Deterministic, cacheable, and much lighter on the infrastructure than SPARQL for 'I already know the QID' cases.
sources.ring_or_timescale: All rings once a QID is known (building, street, neighborhood, city, county, state, country, continent). Time: whatever is on the item - population and officeholder series by year, inception/dissolution by year/decade/century; precision is encoded per time value (precision 7 = century, 9 = year, 11 = day), which maps naturally onto the time slider's granularity.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: CORS confirmed from source: Wikibase's EntityDataRequestHandler explicitly sends 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' (line ~207) for Special:EntityData responses; the action API (wbgetentities, wbsearchentities, wbgetclaims) goes through the same ApiMain origin=* path as Wikipedia's API; Phabricator T150290 added CORS to the whole redirect chain from https://www.wikidata.org/entity/Q... . wikibase-sdk (browser-capable) builds exactly these URLs. Limits: wbgetentities accepts at most 50 ids per call; keep props= tight (claims can be several MB for country items like Q30 - prefer SPARQL or wbgetclaims&property=P1082 for countries); same 2026 global rate limits (200 req/min browser tier) and User-Agent policy as the other action APIs; Special:EntityData is edge-cached and fine to hit per item.
sources.license_attribution: CC0 1.0 for all Wikidata statements, labels and descriptions; images referenced via P18 are Commons files with their own licenses.
sources.notes: Recommended as the backbone lookup: geocoder -> QIDs (OSM wikidata tags or wbsearchentities) -> wbgetentities for the ring items -> sitelinks.enwiki.title for Wikipedia text -> claims.P373 for Commons category -> claims.P2184 for the 'History of X' item (its sitelink is the article). Time values come as '+1790-07-16T00:00:00Z' with a precision field; negative years are BCE.

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons geosearch + imageinfo/extmetadata (photos near a point with creation dates, authors and licenses)
sources.example_request:
Photos within 500 m (camera OR subject coordinates), with thumbnail, date, author, license in ONE call:
https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&format=json&formatversion=2&origin=*&generator=geosearch&ggscoord=38.8977|-77.0365&ggsradius=500&ggslimit=50&ggsnamespace=6&ggsprimary=all&prop=imageinfo|coordinates&coprimary=all&iiprop=url|timestamp|extmetadata&iiurlwidth=640&iiextmetadatafilter=DateTimeOriginal|DateTime|Artist|Credit|LicenseShortName|LicenseUrl|AttributionRequired|Copyrighted|ImageDescription|ObjectName|Categories

Decade-bucketed historical photos of the city ring via Commons categories (old photos usually have no camera coordinates):
https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&format=json&formatversion=2&origin=*&generator=categorymembers&gcmtitle=Category:Washington,_D.C._in_the_1890s&gcmtype=file&gcmlimit=50&prop=imageinfo&iiprop=url|extmetadata&iiurlwidth=480&iiextmetadatafilter=DateTimeOriginal|Artist|LicenseShortName|LicenseUrl|Credit

Full-text/category search in the file namespace: https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&format=json&origin=*&list=search&srnamespace=6&srlimit=50&srsearch=deepcat:%22History%20of%20Washington,%20D.C.%22
sources.what_it_gives: Every Commons file with GeoData coordinates inside the radius (ggsprimary=all includes 'object location' coordinates, which is what old photos of a building typically carry), with direct thumbnail URLs on upload.wikimedia.org (thumburl via iiurlwidth), the file description page URL (descriptionurl) and extmetadata: DateTimeOriginal (creation date from the {{Information}} template or EXIF - the CommonsMetadata extension normalizes it to ISO 'YYYY-MM-DD[ HH:MM:SS]' when it can, otherwise it is free text, possibly with HTML), DateTime (last upload/modification), Artist, Credit, LicenseShortName/LicenseUrl, AttributionRequired, Copyrighted, ImageDescription, Categories. Sort or bucket photos by the year parsed from DateTimeOriginal to drive the time slider. Decade categories ('<City> in the 1890s', '<City> in the 20th century', 'Historical images of <City>') and deepcat:/incategory: searches cover the many historical photos that have no coordinates at all.
sources.ring_or_timescale: Rings: house/street/neighborhood (radius 100-500 m), city (radius up to 10 km or decade categories), county/state/country (category trees only; geosearch is pointless at that scale). Time: photographs/engravings/maps from the 1840s onward (the bulk is 2005+), prints and paintings earlier for major cities; no deep time.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: CORS: same origin=* mechanism as every MediaWiki action API (ApiMain source). Browser-side open-source proof: Viglino/ol-ext WikiCommons.js (OpenLayers source) requests 'https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&format=json&origin=*&prop=coordinates|imageinfo&generator=geosearch&iiprop=...|extmetadata|...&iiextmetadatafilter=LicenseShortName...&ggsnamespace=6' and reads extmetadata.LicenseShortName; wladich/nakarte (nakarte.me Leaflet app) uses origin=*&generator=geosearch&ggsprimary=all&ggsnamespace=6 with prop=imageinfo|coordinates and iiprop=url|mime|size|extmetadata and reads extmetadata.DateTimeOriginal / DateTime / Artist / ImageDescription / ObjectName for captions; tbo47/ez-opendata does list=geosearch&gsbbox=...&gsnamespace=6 and prop=imageinfo&iiprop=extmetadata|url. CommonsMetadata DataCollector::normalizeMetadataTimestamps normalizes 'DateTime' and 'DateTimeOriginal'. Limits: gsradius 10..10000 m, gslimit max 500; imageinfo for up to 50 pages per call; same 2026 global rate limits and User-Agent policy. Thumbnails: request a fixed iiurlwidth (e.g. 320/640) and hotlink the returned thumburl; do not hotlink full-resolution originals and do not generate thousands of odd sizes.
sources.license_attribution: Per file, never blanket: most are CC BY / CC BY-SA / CC0 / public domain, some Fair-use-free but 'AttributionRequired'. Commons' reuse guidance expects a caption with author (Artist), license name with link (LicenseShortName/LicenseUrl) and a link back to the file page (descriptionurl). Old (pre-1930 US / author-died-70-years) images are usually PD and still deserve the source link.
sources.notes: DateTimeOriginal is messy: expect '1898', 'circa 1910', 'between 1900 and 1920', HTML <time> wrappers, or missing; parse the first 4-digit year with a regex and treat unparseable values as undated. Many 19th-century photos carry only an object-location (secondary) coordinate or none, so combine geosearch (ggsprimary=all) with category browsing keyed off Wikidata P373 of each ring item and decade subcategories. A CirrusSearch 'nearcoord:<radius>,<lat>,<lon>' keyword exists in MediaWiki search help but I could not verify its availability on Commons from here - treat as unverified.

sources.name: Wikimedia Commons Structured Data (MediaInfo entities via wbgetentities on M-ids, plus haswbstatement search)
sources.example_request:
Step 1 - find files that depict a ring item (White House Q35525) regardless of coordinates:
https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?action=query&format=json&formatversion=2&origin=*&list=search&srnamespace=6&srlimit=50&srsearch=haswbstatement:P180=Q35525

Step 2 - read structured data for up to 50 of those files (MediaInfo id = 'M' + pageid):
https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/api.php?action=wbgetentities&ids=M82858744|M12345&props=claims|labels&languages=en&format=json&origin=*
 -> claims.P571 (inception = when the photo/print was made, as a Wikibase time value with precision), P180 depicts (QIDs), P1259 point of view / P9149 coordinates of depicted place, P275 license (QID), P6216 copyright status, P170 creator, P7482 source of file
sources.what_it_gives: Machine-readable creation dates (P571 time values with explicit precision: year, decade, century) that are far cleaner than extmetadata free text, 'depicts' links from files to the Wikidata items of your rings (so you can find photos of a building, street, neighborhood or city that have no coordinates), license/copyright as QIDs, and depicted-place coordinates. haswbstatement:P180=Qnn in CirrusSearch gives the file list without needing the Commons SPARQL service. Depicts is used on more than 28 million files (2026); P571 coverage is lower but growing via batch tools.
sources.ring_or_timescale: All rings that have a Wikidata item (building, street, neighborhood, city, county, state, country). Time: year/decade-precision creation dates for historical images from the 1800s onward; no deep time.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: CORS: wbgetentities and list=search are ordinary action-API modules, so origin=* works exactly as proven in ApiMain.php; I found no browser-side open-source project doing wbgetentities on M-ids specifically, hence 'medium'. The 'M' + pageid convention and wbgetentities&ids=M... usage are documented (Wikibase/API, Commons:Structured data, the byabbe.se walkthrough). haswbstatement:P180=Q... is the documented WikibaseCirrusSearch keyword used by Commons MediaSearch, not live-verified here. Limits: 50 ids per wbgetentities call; srlimit max 500 (50 for anonymous-friendly paging); same 2026 global rate limits. Hard limitation: the Commons SPARQL service (WCQS, commons-query.wikimedia.org) requires an OAuth login, so a static site cannot use it - this API-based route is the substitute.
sources.license_attribution: Structured data on Commons is CC0; the files themselves keep their per-file license (read P275/P6216 here or LicenseShortName from imageinfo) and must be credited per Commons reuse guidance.
sources.notes: Pipeline: Wikidata QID of a ring item -> haswbstatement:P180=QID search (optionally add 'filetype:bitmap' and sort=create_timestamp_asc) -> pageids -> wbgetentities M-ids -> read P571 and bucket by year/decade for the time slider; fall back to imageinfo extmetadata DateTimeOriginal when P571 is absent. Time values look like {time:'+1898-00-00T00:00:00Z', precision:9} - precision 9 = year, 8 = decade, 7 = century.

gaps: 1) Granularity: Wikipedia/Wikidata/Commons have nothing for an ordinary house, lot or block, and very little for individual streets outside big cities; the innermost rings get data only when the address is near an NRHP/heritage-listed building or a named landmark. Expect the 'house' and 'street' rings to be empty for most suburban/rural addresses and to fall through to the neighborhood or town ring. 2) No map geometry through time: these sources give narrative text, dates and photos, not historical boundaries, street layouts or land cover; the 'surroundings change as you drag the date' map needs other sources (OpenHistoricalMap, historical topo/aerial imagery, Macrostrat/GPlates for deep time). 3) Time coverage stops at written history: year-by-year detail exists only where editors wrote it (population by census year, mayors, 'History of <City>' decade sections); historical P131/P17 qualifiers in Wikidata are sparse outside Europe, so 'which polity was this in 1750?' is unreliable from Wikidata alone; nothing for millennia-to-eons except a few 'Geology of <region>' articles. 4) Photo dating is weak: extmetadata DateTimeOriginal is free text and often missing, old photos usually lack camera coordinates, and the cleaner structured P571 dates cover only a fraction of files; the Commons SPARQL service (WCQS) needs an OAuth login and so cannot be used from a static site. 5) Nothing here was live-verified: every Wikimedia host (wikipedia, wikidata, commons, mediawiki.org, meta, lists, phabricator and even mirrors) was blocked by the sandbox egress proxy, so all claims rest on source code fetched from GitHub mirrors (MediaWiki core ApiMain/CorsUtils/MainConfigSchema, Wikibase EntityDataRequestHandler, mobileapps app.js, WMF InitialiseSettings) plus browser-side open-source projects and search snippets of the policy pages; the 2026 rate-limit numbers (200 req/min browser, 10 req/min unidentified) come from search snippets and a GitHub issue quoting the policy, and WMF labels them 'subject to experimentation and change'. 6) Header hygiene traps: a browser cannot set User-Agent; Api-User-Agent is CORS-whitelisted on the Action API only - sending it to /api/rest_v1 or query.wikidata.org fails the preflight (T362570), so those must be plain GETs. 7) English-only bias: the examples use en.wikipedia; for non-English places use the sitelinks from Wikidata to pick the local-language wiki (same APIs, same CORS). 8) Text license obligations: CC BY-SA 4.0 requires visible attribution and share-alike on adapted text; summarizing or rewriting Wikipedia text in the UI makes the rewritten text share-alike too.
recommendation: Use Wikidata as the spine and Wikipedia/Commons as the flesh, in this order. (1) After geocoding, resolve each ring to a Wikidata QID (OSM wikidata tags from the geocoder where available, otherwise one wikibase:around SPARQL query with radius 0.3-1 km for the inner rings and wdt:P131+ from the nearest settlement for the outer rings). (2) Fetch the ring items with one wbgetentities call (<=50 ids, props=labels|descriptions|claims|sitelinks, sitefilter=enwiki|commonswiki): it is CC0, cached, CORS-enabled from source, and it hands you everything else - inception/dissolution, population-by-year (P1082/P585) for the time slider, named-after, NRHP/heritage flags, the enwiki title, the Commons category (P373) and the 'History of X' item (P2184). (3) For text, call the Wikipedia Action API with origin=* : one generator=geosearch call (ggsradius 300-1000 m, coprop=type, ppprop=wikibase_item, exintro extracts) for nearby buildings/landmarks, one prop=extracts|pageprops call for the outer-ring titles, then action=parse&prop=sections + section=N (or REST page/html sliced by data-mw-section-id) to show the History section, and the P2184/hatnote 'History of <City>' article as plain text with exsectionformat=wiki so decade headings can be aligned with the time slider. Use REST page/summary for the lightweight cards and thumbnails (no custom headers). (4) For images, call Commons generator=geosearch (ggsnamespace=6, ggsprimary=all, iiprop=url|extmetadata, iiurlwidth=640) for the inner rings and decade categories / haswbstatement:P180=QID + wbgetentities M-ids for city-and-up rings, bucket by parsed year, and always render author + license + file-page link. Why this order: Wikidata is cheapest and CC0, gives stable keys to dedupe across the three systems, and one entity call replaces many Wikipedia lookups; SPARQL is the only piece with real capacity limits (60 s, 5 parallel/IP, 429 bans), so keep it to 1-2 small LIMITed queries per address and cache by QID in IndexedDB. Request hygiene for a static site: formatversion=2, origin=* on every action-API call, redirects=1, batch titles/ids up to 50, send requests serially, honor 429 Retry-After, never add User-Agent/Api-User-Agent to REST or WDQS calls (add Api-User-Agent only on action-API calls if you want), and keep one visitor's traffic well under the 200 req/min browser tier (an address load should be ~6-10 requests). Verify live before shipping (task #3): confirm the Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers on en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php, /api/rest_v1/page/summary, query.wikidata.org/sparql and commons.wikimedia.org, and confirm haswbstatement: search and the current numbers on mediawiki.org/wiki/Wikimedia_APIs/Rate_limits. Evidence copies of all grepped sources are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-sno-ball/a6069c2d-56e0-5914-9c8c-c420aa5c5797/scratchpad/gh/.

sources.name: OpenHistoricalMap vector tiles + official MapLibre styles + @openhistoricalmap/maplibre-gl-dates
sources.example_request: Style (self-contained on GitHub Pages, sprite+glyphs included): https://openhistoricalmap.github.io/map-styles/main/main.json  — tile for lat 38.8977 lon -77.0365 at z15: https://vtiles.openhistoricalmap.org/maps/osm/15/9371/12536.pbf  — JS: import {filterByDate} from '@openhistoricalmap/maplibre-gl-dates'; map.once('styledata',()=>filterByDate(map,'1850'))
sources.what_it_gives: Global vector tiles of OHM's historical features (roads/railways, buildings, landuse, water, boundaries incl. historical countries/states via land_ohm_lines/land_ohm_centroids, place labels). Every feature carries start_date/end_date (strings) and start_decdate/end_decdate (decimal years) so one tileset serves all dates; the plugin rewrites every layer filter at runtime to ['all',['any',['all',['has','start_decdate'],['<','start_decdate',END]],...],['any',['all',['has','end_decdate'],['>=','end_decdate',START]],...]] (features lacking dates are kept). Date strings YYYY, YYYY-MM, YYYY-MM-DD; negative years allowed (-0999); proleptic Gregorian, no year 0 (decimal 1.0 = 1 Jan 1 CE, 0.0 = 1 BCE). Four official styles: main/main.json (Historical, 231 layers, 25 source-layers e.g. transport_lines, landuse_areas, water_lines, buildings, place_points, land_ohm_lines), rail/rail.json (Railway), woodblock/woodblock.json, japanese_scroll/ohm-japanese-scroll-map.json. Production site serves the same at https://www.openhistoricalmap.org/map-styles/{main/main,rail/rail,woodblock/woodblock,japanese_scroll/ohm-japanese-scroll-map}.json. The staging branch renames them historical/historical.json, railway/railway.json, japanese_scroll/japanese_scroll.json and switches sources to /maps/ohm/, /maps/ne/ (Natural Earth), /maps/osm_land/ and hillshade https://static-tiles.openhistoricalmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png (staging style has localhost glyph/sprite URLs, so use the main branch or the www copy). Backend is now Martin + Varnish behind Cloudflare Tunnel (ohm-deploy values.production: tilerServerMartin enabled, legacy tilerServer disabled).
sources.ring_or_timescale: Street/neighborhood/city/region/country rings; years to centuries (c. 3000 BCE to present; density is overwhelmingly 1600-2000 CE). Does not cover deep time.
sources.license_attribution: Data and official styles are CC0 1.0 (OHM copyright page / wiki OpenHistoricalMap/License); a few individual features are CC BY / CC BY-SA per license=* tags. Attribution not legally required but requested; the official embed uses customAttribution 'OpenHistoricalMap'. Hillshade raster is separate (check static-tiles source).
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: No published numeric limit; tiles are Varnish-cached behind Cloudflare and offered for third-party reuse (wiki 'Reuse' page; map-styles README tells users to load the style in maputnik.github.io). Be a good citizen: cache, don't bulk-download, show attribution.
sources.notes: CORS evidence: embed.openhistoricalmap.org (GitHub Pages, CNAME file) is a different origin from www.openhistoricalmap.org (style) and vtiles.openhistoricalmap.org (tiles) and loads both with plain MapLibre fetches; OHM documents loading the style into maputnik.github.io, a third-party origin. GitHub Pages copy (openhistoricalmap.github.io) sends ACAO:* like all GitHub Pages. Coverage sparsity: ohmdash reports (2 Oct 2026) 7.6M dated elements, ~2.5M buildings, 632k railroad miles, 2,257 contributors — roughly three orders of magnitude sparser than OSM; expect many places to show only boundaries, major roads/railways and a handful of buildings. Plugin v1.4.0 (CC0, peer maplibre-gl >=3.0.0); official embed pins maplibre-gl ^5.24.0 while npm latest is 6.13.0 (published 2026-10-06) — test the plugin against 6.x. Also @americana/diplomat is used by the embed for label localization (name_$1 properties).

sources.name: OpenHistoricalMap Overpass API and Nominatim (date-aware feature queries and historical geocoding)
sources.example_request: https://overpass-api.openhistoricalmap.org/api/interpreter?data=[out:json][timeout:25];(nwr(around:300,38.8977,-77.0365)["start_date"];);out tags center;   — geocode: https://nominatim.openhistoricalmap.org/search?q=Washington&format=jsonv2  — reverse: https://nominatim.openhistoricalmap.org/reverse?lat=38.8977&lon=-77.0365&format=jsonv2
sources.what_it_gives: Overpass: full OHM database with attic/history metadata (OVERPASS_META: attic) and minute replication; lets you pull every dated feature near a point with its start_date/end_date/name tags to generate ring text ('this block had a brewery 1872-1931'). Nominatim: OHM-specific instance (mediagis/nominatim 5.3.2 image with OHM fork + DateFunctions-plpgsql) so you can search historical place names; standard Nominatim API (/search, /reverse, /lookup, format=jsonv2|geojson).
sources.ring_or_timescale: House/block/street/neighborhood rings (feature-level), years to centuries.
sources.license_attribution: CC0 data (same as tiles); credit OpenHistoricalMap.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: Production config sets OVERPASS_RATE_LIMIT: 2 (concurrent requests per IP) and OVERPASS_ALLOW_DUPLICATE_QUERIES: no (identical back-to-back queries are rejected — see issues #718). No published Nominatim limit; the OHM website itself still geocodes against nominatim.openstreetmap.org (settings.yml nominatim_url), so treat the OHM instance as best-effort.
sources.notes: CORS caveat is real: GitHub issue #1318 'Overpass, CORS and cloudflare' (opened Mar 2026) reports browser Overpass queries broken by Cloudflare's strict CORS handling, plus nosniff + text/html mimetype on JSON responses; a user got it working by adjusting request headers (plain GET, no custom headers that trigger preflight). overpass-turbo.openhistoricalmap.org is a browser client that targets this API, so it is intended to be browser-callable, but build with a fallback (hide the ring text, not the map) and prefer simple GET requests with data= in the query string. OHM also runs a QLever SPARQL endpoint (wiki Reuse page) if Overpass stays flaky. sources.what_it_gives: Full-planet OpenMapTiles-schema vector tiles (z0-14 + overzoom) generated weekly with Planetiler, served as static files from Btrfs images via nginx on two dedicated servers; MapLibre-ready styles liberty, bright, positron (documented) plus dark and fiord (styles repo), fonts at https://tiles.openfreemap.org/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf, sprites at /sprites/ofm_f384/ofm, Natural Earth shaded relief raster at /natural_earth/ne2sr/{z}/{x}/{y}.png. votes.reasoning:

EXISTENCE: Both repos are actively maintained as of this week (openfreemap HEAD f76573c, 2026-10-04; openfreemap-styles HEAD cf9e8e7, 2026-10-06). The website's Terms of Service in-repo is dated 'Last Updated: September 9, 2026' and docs/tilegen_release_cadence.md documents a planet run from 2026-05-26, so the public instance is being operated in 2026. The nginx templates define exactly the claimed routes: `location /styles/ { alias .../assets/styles/ofm/; try_files $uri.json =404; sub_filter '__TILEJSON_DOMAIN__' '__DOMAIN__'; }` (so /styles/liberty serves liberty.json with the host substituted), `location = /{area}` for the latest TileJSON (/planet), a wildcard `location ~ ^/{area}/([^/]+)/(.+)$` that serves /planet/latest/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf from the active Btrfs mount, plus `location /fonts/`, `location /sprites/`, `location /natural_earth/`. The styles repo has bright, dark, fiord, liberty, positron, every one with sprite `https://__TILEJSON_DOMAIN__/sprites/ofm_f384/ofm`, glyphs `https://__TILEJSON_DOMAIN__/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`, and raster source `https://__TILEJSON_DOMAIN__/natural_earth/ne2sr/{z}/{x}/{y}.png`; sprites/sprites/ofm_f384/{ofm.json,ofm.png,ofm@2x.*} exist; liberty uses font stacks Noto Sans Regular/Bold/Italic. website/content/how_to_use/maplibre.md's quick start is literally `style: 'https://tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/liberty'`, and docs/inspecting_tiles.md links Maputnik to tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/{bright,liberty,positron}. The styles README confirms /styles/dark and /styles/fiord exist but are 'not offered on the Quick Start guide'.

CORS: linux_host/linux_host_lib/nginx_config_gen.py defines `PUBLIC_HEADERS = "add_header 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' '*' always; add_header Cache-Control public; ..."` and injects it into every public location: /styles/, /fonts/, /sprites/, /natural_earth/, the specific/latest/wildcard TileJSON blocks, the PBF blocks, and the @empty_tile fallbacks. docs/self_hosting.md shows a sample response with `access-control-allow-origin: *`. It is a bare wildcard (no Allow-Headers/Methods), which is sufficient because MapLibre's fetches are simple GETs with no preflight. The README explicitly says MapHub has used the public instance as its production basemap since June 2024, i.e. cross-origin browser use is the designed purpose.

API KEY: README and website/content/index/whatis.md: 'no limits on the number of map views or requests... no registration, no user database, no API keys, and no cookies.' The nginx config has no auth_basic, auth_request, limit_req, limit_conn, or valid_referers; the only deny is a catch-all `location / { return 403; }` for unknown paths. Tilegen runs Planetiler's default OpenMapTiles profile with no --maxzoom override (default 0-14) and the TileJSON writer copies minzoom/maxzoom from MBTiles metadata, consistent with 'z0-14 + overzoom'. Weekly cadence (Sunday build, Tuesday publish), 2 linux_host servers on round-robin DNS, Btrfs images, and the btrfs.openfreemap.com/files.txt index are all stated in the README/docs. The TileJSON writer hard-codes the attribution string 'OpenFreeMap © OpenMapTiles Data from OpenStreetMap'.

sources.name: Allmaps (georeferenced IIIF historic maps: XYZ tile proxy at allmaps.xyz, annotations API, and client-side WarpedMapLayer for MapLibre)
sources.example_request: https://allmaps.xyz/15/9371/12536.png?url=https://annotations.allmaps.org/maps/9845523343c39447  (or short form https://allmaps.xyz/maps/{mapId}/15/9371/12536.png, optional &transformation.type=thin-plate-spline; TileJSON at https://allmaps.xyz/manifests/{manifestId}/tiles.json) — annotation lookup for any IIIF map you know: https://annotations.allmaps.org/?url={IIIF image or manifest URL}
sources.what_it_gives: Turns any Georeference Annotation (W3C/IIIF georef extension) into a standard XYZ raster layer you can drop under/over the OHM vector layer — this is the practical way to show an 1880 Sanborn/plat/topo sheet of the actual block. sources.ring_or_timescale: House/block/street/neighborhood/city rings; years to centuries (c. 1600-1950 is where most georeferenced sheets sit; US cities 1850-1930 densest via Sanborn/USGS/LOC).
sources.license_attribution: Allmaps software GPL-3.0 (tile server runs on Cloudflare Workers, free public instance). The imagery license is whatever the holding institution grants — LOC/NYPL/USGS sheets are mostly public domain; David Rumsey images are CC BY-NC-SA 3.0; always show the source institution + a link to the IIIF manifest.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: No published limits; allmaps.xyz is a community-run Cloudflare Worker (issue #638 shows occasional broken/empty tiles vs. the Viewer). Treat as best-effort: cache tile URLs, limit to one or two overlays at a time.

The annotations API (https://annotations.allmaps.org/docs) is keyed by IIIF URL/ID; the 'Allmaps Here' app (shows maps around your location) only configures PUBLIC_ANNOTATIONS_URL=https://annotations.allmaps.org, which implies a spatial query exists there but its parameter name (likely intersects= or bbox=) is unverified; @allmaps/render exposes getMapsByGeoBbox client-side. Plan for a curated list of annotation IDs per region (or a small precomputed index) rather than relying on a live spatial search until it is verified. Tiles are PNG images so even without CORS they would display in a raster source; CORS only matters if you read pixels.

sources.license_attribution: USGS maps are US public domain; credit 'USGS Historical Topographic Map Collection' (and Esri for hosting the Living Atlas service).

sources.license_attribution: Most G&M items are public domain (no known restrictions) but rights vary per item — read each item's 'rights' field; credit 'Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division'.

sources.example_request: https://tile.openstreetmap.org/15/9371/12536.png  (MapLibre raster source, tileSize 256, maxzoom 19; must send a real Referer — set <meta name="referrer" content="strict-origin-when-cross-origin"> — and show attribution)
sources.what_it_gives: The familiar OSM Carto map, z0-19, no key, worldwide. Only use as a cheap fallback or for the lowest-traffic case; it cannot be restyled and does not support the OHM date filter.
sources.ring_or_timescale: All spatial rings, present day only.
sources.license_attribution: ODbL data, CC BY-SA style: '© OpenStreetMap contributors' with link to openstreetmap.org/copyright is mandatory; missing attribution gets the referrer blocked.
