gaps: (1) Nothing here was live-tested: every CORS=yes above is inferred from documented cross-origin use (OHM embed on GitHub Pages, Maputnik, MapHub, TopoExplorer), not from observed headers; verify once network access opens, especially OHM Overpass (open Cloudflare CORS issue #1318, Mar 2026), OHM Nominatim, loc.gov JSON, and historical1.arcgis.com token requirement. (2) OHM is sparse: ~7.6M dated elements worldwide vs billions in OSM, so for most addresses the 'back in time' map will show the house/block ring empty and only major roads, railways and admin boundaries; the ring text must say 'no mapped features yet' rather than imply nothing existed. Nothing in this domain covers deep time (millennia to eons): OHM/Allmaps/USGS/LOC stop around 3000 BCE at the very earliest and are really 1600-2000 CE; plate reconstructions, paleogeography and geology need the separate GPlates/Macrostrat/paleo-coastline research. (3) No verified 'which historic map covers this lat/lon' API for Allmaps; Map Warper's bbox search is documented but the NYPL instance is archived; USGS query-by-point works only in the US; LOC search is textual and capped at 20 req/min. Expect to curate a small per-region index of annotation/map IDs. (4) David Rumsey/Georeferencer tiles require a Georeferencer key (WMTS/XYZ ?key=) and are CC BY-NC-SA, so they are out unless you georeference Rumsey's IIIF images yourself via Allmaps. (5) Esri World Imagery is technically fetchable key-free at https://server.arcgisonline.com/ArcGIS/rest/services/World_Imagery/MapServer/tile/{z}/{y}/{x} but Esri's terms call for an ArcGIS key and 'Powered by Esri' attribution (only OSM editing use is explicitly free), so it is a gray area; Stadia (200k credits/mo free, non-commercial, domain-based auth so no secret in code) and MapTiler (free non-commercial plan, key in URL with allowed origins) both need signup and are omitted from the top list. (6) OHM's hillshade raster, Natural Earth source and staging style renames (historical/railway/japanese_scroll) are in flux; pin to the GitHub main-branch style URL and re-check quarterly. (7) OSM raster is policy-limited (no numeric quota; 'heavy use' banned, Referer + User-Agent + attribution + 7-day caching required) — fine for a hobby site, wrong as the primary design choice.
recommendation: Build on three sources first, in this order. sources.license_attribution: Service software: GPL-2.0 (README). Shared academic infrastructure (main server on NCI cloud, backups gws1.gplates.org and gws2.gplates.org). README: 'You are welcome to use our servers' but suggests self-hosting (docker run gplates/gws) for heavy use. Be polite: cache coastline GeoJSON per (model,time) and quantize the slider to a fixed set of ages.

sources.example_request: Build step (not per visitor): curl -sS https://raw.githubusercontent.com/i-c-stratigraphy/chart/main/chart.ttl and convert to JSON — each unit looks like: gtsd:Jurassic a skos:Concept ; gts:rank rank:Period ; skos:broader gtsd:Mesozoic ; skos:narrower gtsd:LowerJurassic ... ; time:hasBeginning [ gtsd:inMYA 201.4 ; schema:marginOfError 0.2 ] ; time:hasEnd [ gtsd:inMYA 143.1 ] ; schema:color "#34B2C9" ; skos:prefLabel "Jurassic"@en. Ready-made (older) JSON alternatives, also raw-fetchable: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TobbeTripitaka/strat2file/master/ChronostratChart2018-08.json (JSON Lines, one row per boundary: Eon, Era, Period, Epoch, Age, Ma, GSSP, Uncertainty; 2018 chart) and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/i-c-stratigraphy/interactive-geological-timescale/master/src/assets/time_interval_data.json ({"...ischart/Jurassic": {hasBeginning, hasEnd}} per unit, GTS2020 numbers). Runtime alternatives with CORS: https://macrostrat.org/api/v2/defs/intervals?timescale=international%20periods or https://paleobiodb.org/data1.2/intervals/list.json?scale=1. For lat=38.8977 lon=-77.0365 the chart is location-independent: given an age (e.g. 200 Ma) pick the eon/era/period/epoch/age whose hasBeginning >= age > hasEnd.
sources.what_it_gives: Authoritative names, hierarchy (eon > era > period > epoch > age), boundary ages in Ma with uncertainties, and official colors for every geologic time unit from the Hadean (4,567 Ma) to the Meghalayan (0.0042 Ma). Drives the labels and colors of the deep-time slider and the 'you are in the Late Jurassic' text.
sources.ring_or_timescale: All rings (it labels time, not space). Time scales: 4,200 years (Holocene ages) through 4.6 billion years (eons).
sources.license_attribution: i-c-stratigraphy/chart: '(c) International Commission on Stratigraphy, 2026 ... licensed for use with the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license' (README.adoc; LICENSE file is CC BY 4.0). strat2file: 'All rights belong to International Commission on Stratigraphy' (no explicit CC grant, 2018 data). interactive-geological-timescale code is GPL-3; its JSON is ICS data.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: None; vendor the converted JSON (~20-120 KB) into the site at build time rather than fetching the 642 KB Turtle file per visitor. raw.githubusercontent.com serves Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * if you do fetch at runtime.
sources.notes: chart.ttl was fetched successfully from raw.githubusercontent.com here (HTTP 200, 642,198 bytes) and the i-c-stratigraphy/chart repo was cloned; the README confirms it is 'the authoritative data of the Chronostratigraphic Chart'. The repo's queries/ folder has get-eons/eras/periods/epochs SPARQL files you can reuse in a small Python/Node build script to emit JSON. The interactive timescale app is retired (README note, Feb 2025) and its numbers are GTS2020-era; the strat2file JSON is the 2018 chart.

sources.name: PALEOMAP / Scotese paleogeography (PaleoDEMs, PaleoCoastlines) and the Ancient Earth globe
sources.example_request: Build step: download the Scotese & Wright (2018) PaleoDEM netCDF/CSV bundle from https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5460860 (117 grids, 1x1 degree, every 5 Myr from 0-540 Ma; also 0.1-degree versions) and the PaleoMAP PaleoCoastlines shapefiles (Kocsis & Scotese, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3903164 / https://zenodo.org/records/4297693), then pre-compute per time step a small JSON such as {"age":200, "elevation_m": <value sampled at the GPlates-reconstructed paleo-position of 38.8977,-77.0365>, "env": "lowland|shallow sea|deep ocean|mountains"} and convert the coastline shapefiles to simplified GeoJSON (e.g. ogr2ogr -f GeoJSON -simplify 0.1) served as static files from your own GitHub Pages origin. The live globe https://dinosaurpictures.org/ancient-earth#200 has no public API; the open-source predecessor https://github.com/typpo/ancient-earth (MIT code) is a three.js globe wrapped around per-age JPEG textures.
sources.what_it_gives: Pretty paleogeographic imagery and elevation/bathymetry through the Phanerozoic: was the spot deep ocean, shallow sea, coastal lowland or mountains at a given age; land/sea coastline polygons every 5 Myr; and the style of globe the user has probably seen ('Ancient Earth'). The GWS PALEOMAP model (Coastlines + StaticPolygons, 0-1100 Ma) is the browser-callable version of the same Scotese plate model.
sources.ring_or_timescale: Rings: continent/plate (1-degree ~100 km cells). Time scales: 5 Myr steps, 0-540 Ma (Phanerozoic); Ancient Earth shows 750 Ma to 0.
sources.license_attribution: PaleoDEMs: EarthByte page says users are 'welcome to freely use the 1 x 1 degree paleoDEMS for your own research projects, presentations, and publications' with citation of Scotese & Wright (2018); secondary sources (R chronosphere/via docs) report the Zenodo records as CC BY 4.0 — Zenodo and earthbyte.org were blocked from this sandbox, so confirm on the record page before redistributing derived files. Ancient Earth / PALEOMAP globe images: scotese.com/license.htm permits non-commercial personal and academic/educational use with credit to 'C.R. Scotese, PALEOMAP Project' and forbids copying, reselling or commercial use without a written license — do not scrape or rehost dinosaurpictures.org textures. typpo/ancient-earth code is MIT but its textures are 'courtesy of Northern Arizona University' (Ron Blakey maps, separately copyrighted) and are not redistributable.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: Downloads only (no API). Zenodo files are fine to fetch once at build time; never hot-link them from the visitor's browser. Keep derived static assets small (the 1-degree DEMs are 65k cells each; quantize to a few hundred KB per age or sample only along the point's paleo-path).
sources.notes: The Ancient Earth globe credits 'plate tectonic and paleogeographic maps by C.R. Scotese, PALEOMAP Project' and reconstructs the typed city with GPlates — i.e. exactly the GPlates WS + PALEOMAP combination above, so you can reproduce its behaviour legally with GWS (model=PALEOMAP) for geometry and your own rendering for colour. 'via' R package man page confirms the PaleoCoastlines dataset (Kocsis & Scotese, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.3903164) is derived from the PaleoDEMs plus PBDB.

sources.name: Quaternary ice sheets, sea level and paleoclimate (PaleoMIST 1.0, Dyke 2003 / Batchelor 2019 ice margins, Spratt & Lisiecki sea-level stack, CHELSA-TraCE21k / PaleoClim)
sources.example_request: Build step, then static JSON on your own origin: (1) PaleoMIST 1.0 (Gowan et al. 2021, Pangaea 905800): ice-margin shapefiles + paleotopography netCDF (1 and 0.25 degree) every 2.5 kyr for 80 ka-0 -> ogr2ogr to simplified GeoJSON per time slice, sample paleotopography at 38.8977,-77.0365 to answer 'ice / dry land / sea' per step. (2) North America only, GitHub-hosted: https://github.com/awickert/North-American-Ice-Sheets (Dyke et al. 2003 ice + proglacial lakes, WGS84 shapefiles per radiocarbon age, e.g. WGS84/ice018000/...). (3) Northern Hemisphere LGM/MIS stages: Batchelor et al. 2019 shapefiles at https://osf.io/7jen3/. (4) Global sea level vs. time: Spratt & Lisiecki 2016 stack, NOAA paleo study 19982 (https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/paleo/study/19982; also packaged in https://github.com/benmarwick/gsloid) -> a ~1,600-row {age_ka, sea_level_m} JSON; combine with the point's present elevation to say 'the coast was X km farther out'. (5) Climate at a point: CHELSA-TraCE21k (https://www.envidat.ch/dataset/chelsa_trace, 30 arcsec monthly tas/pr in 100-yr steps for 21 ka-0) or PaleoClim (http://www.paleoclim.org, LGM/mid-Holocene/Pliocene/Pleistocene slices at 2.5-10 arcmin) -> pre-sample temperature/precip for a coarse global grid (e.g. 0.5 degree) into static tiles/JSON.
sources.what_it_gives: For the 'thousands of years' part of the slider: whether the spot was under an ice sheet, next to a proglacial lake, dry land or sea at each step from 80 ka (or 21 ka) to present; global sea-level offset for every millennium; and approximate annual temperature/precipitation for the LGM and later slices.
sources.ring_or_timescale: Rings: city/county through continent (1 degree to 30 arcsec grids; Dyke/Batchelor polygons are regional-scale). Time scales: 100-year to 2,500-year steps across 21-80 ka; sea level in ~1 kyr steps to 800 ka.
sources.license_attribution: PaleoMIST on PANGAEA: PANGAEA datasets are open access under Creative Commons (normally CC BY 4.0) — Pangaea was not reachable from this sandbox to confirm the exact badge; cite Gowan et al. (2021) Nat. Commun. Dyke 2003 originals: 'copyrighted property of the Geological Survey of Canada, made available for the purposes of study, teaching and research'; A. Wickert releases his WGS84 reprojections freely (repo README) — fine for a non-commercial hobby site with citation of Dyke, Moore & Robertson (2003) GSC Open File 1574. Batchelor 2019 (OSF 7jen3): copyright the authors; license not confirmed here — cite the Nature Communications paper and check the OSF page. Spratt & Lisiecki data on NOAA NCEI: US-government-hosted, free with citation of Spratt & Lisiecki (2016) Clim. Past 12:1079. CHELSA-TraCE21k (EnviDat, doi:10.16904/envidat.211) and PaleoClim (Brown et al. 2018 Sci. Data 5:180254): free for use with citation of both the dataset and underlying models; redistribution of full rasters is not needed if you ship only sampled values.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: All are bulk downloads intended for offline processing; none should be called from the visitor's browser. CHELSA-TraCE21k is tens of GB — sample at build time with a script and commit only the derived JSON. De Groeve et al. 2022 'coastline positions since LGM' raster (UvA figshare doi 10.21942/uva.17215094) is an alternative 26 ka-0 coastline-age raster if you want 'when did this seabed become land'.
sources.notes: No GitHub-hosted ready-made global LGM GeoJSON was found; the only GitHub-native ice dataset located is the Dyke 2003 North American set (shapefiles, radiocarbon ages that must be calibrated). Everything else requires a one-time conversion step, which fits a GitHub Pages site fine (run it in a GitHub Action and commit the outputs). Hosting sites pangaea.de, osf.io, envidat.ch and paleoclim.org were not reachable from this sandbox, so formats and licenses here come from publications, package docs and search summaries.

gaps: Nothing here was live-verified: gws.gplates.org, macrostrat.org, paleobiodb.org, zenodo.org, earthbyte.org, scotese.com, paleoclim.org and r-project.org were all blocked by the egress proxy; CORS and parameter claims rest on the services' own source code (cloned from GitHub) and docs, so a first real browser test is still required. There is no browser-callable 'paleoclimate at a point' API at all — climate (temperature/precipitation) for the LGM/Holocene/Pliocene must be pre-sampled at build time from CHELSA-TraCE21k or PaleoClim rasters. Ice-sheet and sea-level data exist only as shapefile/netCDF downloads (Pangaea/OSF/NOAA), not GeoJSON on GitHub, except the North-America-only Dyke 2003 repo; licenses for PaleoMIST, Batchelor 2019, the PaleoDEMs and PaleoCoastlines could not be read from their record pages and need confirmation before redistributing derivatives. The Ancient Earth globe's imagery is non-commercial-only and has no API; you can reproduce its behaviour with GPlates WS (model=PALEOMAP) but not reuse its textures. Spatial resolution collapses at depth: plate reconstructions and PaleoDEMs are ~1 degree, so the house/block/street rings have no meaningful content older than the bedrock map unit (Macrostrat) — for deep time the rings beyond 'city' all show the same thing. Macrostrat's detailed bedrock mapping is strongest in North America; elsewhere you often get only the small-scale global unit. Time resolution: nothing finer than 1 Myr in plate models and 5 Myr in PaleoDEMs; CAO2024 stops at 1.8 Ga and nothing covers the Hadean/early Archean beyond ICS names and the oldest Macrostrat unit ages. GPlates WS has an unpublished optional per-IP throttle on a shared academic server; PBDB and Macrostrat publish no quota but are small research services, so the site must cache and quantize slider steps rather than firing a request per tick.
recommendation: Start with Macrostrat: one CORS-enabled call (/geologic_units/map?lat&lng, or /mobile/point) answers 'what rock is under this address, how old is it, what environment deposited it' for the whole deep-time range and is CC BY 4.0; use /defs/intervals (or a vendored ICS chart JSON built from i-c-stratigraphy/chart, CC BY 4.0) for eon/era/period names, ages and official colors on the slider. Add GPlates Web Service second for the 'the map changes as you go back' effect: reconstruct_points (model MERDITH2021 to 1,000 Ma, MULLER2019 for best 0-250 Ma detail, CAO2024 to 1.8 Ga) gives the paleo-position and plate id (name it via /earth/get_plate_names), and /reconstruct/coastlines or /map/get_cached_map gives the world at that age; quantize the slider to a fixed list of ages (e.g. every 5-10 Myr) and cache per (model,time); for zero-server-load point reconstruction, load /rotation/get_rotation_map once and rotate client-side with the `gplates` npm package. Add PBDB third (occs/list with a bounding box, vocab=pbdb, show=coords,class,strat) for 'fossils found near here' per period. Treat PALEOMAP PaleoDEMs/PaleoCoastlines and the Quaternary ice/sea-level/climate sets as build-time static derivatives committed to the repo (a GitHub Action can download, sample and simplify them), never as runtime dependencies, and confirm their Zenodo/Pangaea license badges first. Do not scrape Ancient Earth; cite Scotese/PALEOMAP via the GWS PALEOMAP model instead.

sources.name: Library of Congress loc.gov JSON API (Chronicling America newspapers, HABS/HAER/HALS, photos, maps)
sources.example_request: Newspapers (street/neighborhood/city rings, 1770s-1963): https://www.loc.gov/collections/chronicling-america/?qs=%22Pennsylvania+Avenue%22&location_state=district+of+columbia&start_date=1880-01-01&end_date=1899-12-31&dl=page&fo=json&c=10&at=results,pagination  |  HABS/HAER/HALS building surveys (house/block ring): https://www.loc.gov/collections/historic-american-buildings-landscapes-and-engineering-records/?fa=location:washington+d.c.&q=pennsylvania+avenue&fo=json&c=25&at=results,pagination  |  Photos: https://www.loc.gov/photos/?fa=location:washington+d.c.&q=lafayette+square&dates=1900/1950&fo=json&at=results,pagination  |  Maps (Sanborn fire-insurance maps etc.): https://www.loc.gov/maps/?fa=location:washington+d.c.&q=sanborn&fo=json
sources.what_it_gives: Append fo=json to almost any loc.gov page. Search endpoints /search, /{format} (photos, maps, newspapers), /collections/{slug}; filters: q=, qs= (phrase), fa=location:<place>|subject:<x> (facet filter, pipe-separated), dates=YYYY/YYYY, location_state=, start_date/end_date, dl=page, c= (page size), sp= (page), at=results,pagination (trim payload). Newspaper page hits carry OCR text in full_text; items carry title, date, image_url[] (thumbnails/IIIF), location, location_county, subject, and an optional coordinates string ('not universally implemented'). HABS/HAER/HALS has 40,000+ documented structures (measured drawings, large-format photos, written histories) organized by state/county/city. Chronicling America: millions of US newspaper pages, 1770s-1963, moved onto this API (legacy chroniclingamerica.loc.gov API retired Aug 2025). No lat/lon search: you pass the geocoder's place names (street, neighborhood, city, county, state) as q/fa.
sources.ring_or_timescale: house/lot, block, street (HABS, Sanborn maps, newspaper mentions of a street/address), neighborhood, city, county, state; years and decades from ~1770 to 1963 (newspapers), 1933-present (HABS), 1860s-1960s (Sanborn maps, image availability varies)
evidence_urls: https://github.com/storytracer/loc-downloader (api-docs/working-within-limits.md and api-docs/api-request-parameters.md are verbatim copies of the LC docs incl. fa=location examples and the limits table)
sources.license_attribution: No key, no auth; the API itself is free. Most HABS/HAER/HALS and Chronicling America content is public domain (US government work / pre-1930 and cleared pages to 1963); each item carries its own rights statement in the JSON, so show per-item rights and link back to loc.gov. LC asks for attribution 'Library of Congress' with the item URL.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: Documented per-endpoint limits (exceeding = temporary block): item/resource endpoints burst 40 req/10 s (block 5 min), crawl 200 req/min (block 1 h); collections/format/search endpoints burst 20 req/10 s (block 5 min), crawl 80 req/min (block 1 h); newspapers endpoint burst 20 req/min (block 5 min), crawl 20 req/10 s (block 1 h). Under heavy load LC may return 429 or an HTML CAPTCHA page even below the limits, so treat non-JSON responses as a soft failure and back off. No deep paging past 100,000 results; queries with >100k hits are rejected (narrow with dates, state, LCCN). Because limits are per client IP, each visitor's browser gets its own budget, which suits a static site.
sources.notes: Live call not possible from this sandbox (loc.gov blocked by egress proxy); CORS is inferred from at least six independent plain-HTML/JS projects on GitHub that call www.loc.gov?fo=json straight from the browser with no proxy. Use the geocoder's reverse-geocode (street, neighborhood, city, county, state) to build q/fa values; combine qs="" with location_state to get street-level newspaper hits. Image thumbnails (image_url) are plain URLs (no CORS needed). Also useful: /search/index/location/?fa=partof:...&fo=json to list location facets.

sources.name: Wikidata Query Service (SPARQL) + Wikidata action API — events, buildings, streets, name origins near a point
sources.example_request: GET https://query.wikidata.org/sparql?format=json&query=SELECT%20%3Fitem%20%3FitemLabel%20%3Fdate%20%3FtypeLabel%20%3Fdist%20WHERE%20%7B%20SERVICE%20wikibase%3Aaround%20%7B%20%3Fitem%20wdt%3AP625%20%3Fcoord%20.%20bd%3AserviceParam%20wikibase%3Acenter%20%22Point(-77.0365%2038.8977)%22%5E%5Egeo%3AwktLiteral%20%3B%20wikibase%3Aradius%20%221.5%22%20%3B%20wikibase%3Adistance%20%3Fdist%20.%20%7D%20%7B%20%3Fitem%20wdt%3AP585%20%3Fdate%20%7D%20UNION%20%7B%20%3Fitem%20wdt%3AP571%20%3Fdate%20%7D%20OPTIONAL%20%7B%20%3Fitem%20wdt%3AP31%20%3Ftype%20%7D%20SERVICE%20wikibase%3Alabel%20%7B%20bd%3AserviceParam%20wikibase%3Alanguage%20%22en%22.%20%7D%20%7D%20ORDER%20BY%20%3Fdate%20LIMIT%20200   (decoded: SELECT ?item ?itemLabel ?date ?typeLabel ?dist WHERE { SERVICE wikibase:around { ?item wdt:P625 ?coord . bd:serviceParam wikibase:center "Point(-77.0365 38.8977)"^^geo:wktLiteral ; wikibase:radius "1.5" ; wikibase:distance ?dist . } { ?item wdt:P585 ?date } UNION { ?item wdt:P571 ?date } OPTIONAL { ?item wdt:P31 ?type } SERVICE wikibase:label { bd:serviceParam wikibase:language "en". } } ORDER BY ?date LIMIT 200)  |  Street name origin for an OSM way tagged name:etymology:wikidata=Q42 (or a Wikidata street item's P138 'named after'): https://www.wikidata.org/w/api.php?action=wbgetentities&ids=Q42&props=labels|descriptions|claims|sitelinks&languages=en&format=json&origin=*
sources.what_it_gives: Every Wikidata item with a coordinate (P625) within a radius, with point in time (P585, events), inception (P571, buildings/streets/towns founded), start/end time (P580/P582), instance-of (P31), named after (P138), image (P18), and sitelinks to Wikipedia. One query returns a dated, geolocated timeline of events + constructions + foundings around the address; order by ?date to drive the time slider. Also resolves the Qid from OSM name:etymology:wikidata / wikidata tags to a person/thing with description and image, giving 'this street is named after ...'. Wikidata graph split (2024-25) moved scholarly articles to a separate graph; geographic and event items remain in the main endpoint.
sources.ring_or_timescale: block, street, neighborhood, city, county, state, country (radius is a parameter: 0.3 km for block, 1-2 km neighborhood, 10-30 km city/county); years to millennia (dates are full xsd:dateTime with precision, BCE supported) — the best single source for the 'events near here by year' feed
sources.license_attribution: Wikidata content is CC0 (no attribution legally required; courteous to link the item). Wikipedia text pulled via sitelinks is CC BY-SA 4.0 (attribute + share-alike if you display excerpts).
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: WDQS: hard query timeout 60 s; one client (User-Agent + IP) gets 60 s of processing time per 60 s and 30 error queries per minute; over-limit returns HTTP 429 with Retry-After. Keep radius small and LIMIT modest so queries finish in a few seconds; cache results per (lat,lon,radius) in localStorage. Browsers cannot set User-Agent, which WDQS tolerates for interactive use (the Origin header identifies you); do not fan out dozens of parallel queries per page load. wikidata.org action API: CORS requires the origin=* query parameter for anonymous requests; standard Wikimedia API etiquette (serial requests, no hammering).
sources.notes: Not live-tested here (wikidata.org blocked by the sandbox proxy); CORS on query.wikidata.org is well established (Open Library's production browser code calls it; Wikimedia documents CORS for the action API via origin=*). Filtering by P585/P571 inside the around-service is fast; avoid wdt:P31/wdt:P279* wd:Q1190554 class walks in the same query (timeouts). For street-name origins in the US coverage is thin: name:etymology:wikidata on OSM ways and P138 on Wikidata street items are dense in parts of Europe (DE, NL, CZ, FR, IT) and sparse in North America, so present it as 'when available'.

EXISTENCE: (1) Wikimedia DNS zone templates/wikidata.org has `query`, `query-main`, `query-scholarly`, `query-next`, `query-scholarly-next` CNAMEs. (2) operations-puppet production hieradata/common/profile/trafficserver/backend.yaml remaps `http://query.wikidata.org/sparql` -> `https://wdqs-main.discovery.wmnet/sparql` (i.e. query.wikidata.org now serves the post-split MAIN graph, consistent with the claim that geographic/event items remain there). (3) The WDQS nginx template rewrites `^/sparql$` to `/bigdata/namespace/<ns>/sparql`, allows only GET/OPTIONS/POST, and sets `X-BIGDATA-MAX-QUERY-MILLIS` from `max_query_time_millis` (default 60000 in profile/query_service/gui.pp) = the 60 s timeout. (4) `SERVICE wikibase:around` with `wikibase:center`, `wikibase:radius`, `wikibase:distance` (plus optional `wikibase:globe`) is implemented in wikidata-query-rdf master GeoAroundService.java and registered/whitelisted in GeoService.java; the example query uses exactly those parameters and the standard wdt:/bd:/geo: prefixes. (5) `?format=json` cross-origin is used in Open Library's production client-side code (readinglog_stats.js: `fetch('https://query.wikidata.org/sparql?format=json', {method:'POST', body:new URLSearchParams({query})}).then(r=>r.json())`; the file also calls document.getElementById, so it is browser code).

CORS / NO KEY: nginx.erb for the query service, non-OAuth branch (hieradata/role/common/wdqs/main.yaml: `profile::query_service::oauth: false`), emits `add_header Access-Control-Allow-Origin * always;` and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers "accept, content-type, content-length, user-agent, api-user-agent"` on the SPARQL location; no auth_request is applied. OAuth/JWT (`wcqsSession`) only applies to the OAuth-protected Commons deployment. For the action API, MediaWiki core includes/api/ApiMain.php (main branch) handleCORS(): `if ($originParam === '*') { $allowOrigin='*'; $allowCredentials='false'; }` then `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: $allowOrigin`, and `origin=*` marks the request anonymous (lacksSameOriginSecurity). keewerner/Websites master RomaLive/map.js does `fetch('https://www.wikidata.org/w/api.php?action=wbgetentities&origin=*&format=json&ids=...')` from the browser. Wikimedia's wgCrossSiteAJAXdomains is only needed for the credentialed (origin=<site>) form.

RATE LIMITS: ThrottlingFilter.java returns HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header, and bans (403, default 24 h) clients that keep ignoring 429s; ThrottlingFilterConfig.java defaults: time bucket capacity 120 s refilled 60 s per minute, error bucket capacity 60 refilled 30 per minute, throttle bucket 200 per 20 min; nginx also enforces `limit_conn byaddr 5` (429) and 403 for an empty User-Agent. The puppet-added JVM opts only toggle `enable-throttling-if-header` (throttle CDN/external traffic only); no overrides of the bucket sizes were found. So the claim's "60 s of processing per 60 s, 30 errors per minute" matches the steady-state refill rates.

Minor inaccuracies noted in corrected_facts (bucketing is by IP + User-Agent, not Origin; burst capacities are 120 s / 60 errors; a parallel 'query-next' backend exists). None affects existence, CORS, or the no-key status.
votes.corrected_facts: 1) Throttling buckets are keyed by remote IP + User-Agent header (UserAgentIpAddressBucketing), or by regex-matched generic agents/queries; the Origin header plays no role. Browsers always send a UA, and only an empty UA is rejected (nginx returns 403). 2) Code defaults: time bucket capacity 120 s refilled at 60 s/min; error bucket capacity 60 refilled at 30/min; throttle bucket 200 per 20 min, after which a 24 h ban (HTTP 403) applies; nginx additionally caps 5 concurrent connections per IP (429). The claim's '60 s per 60 s / 30 errors per minute' is the steady-state rate; bursts up to 120 s / 60 errors are tolerated. 3) query.wikidata.org/sparql is remapped at the CDN to the wdqs-main cluster (main graph without scholarly articles), as the claim says; query-main.wikidata.org and query-scholarly.wikidata.org are separate hostnames, and query-next.wikidata.org / query-scholarly-next.wikidata.org point at a new 'wdqs2' backend — whether that successor keeps the Blazegraph-specific `wikibase:around` SERVICE is unverified, so re-check if query.wikidata.org is later moved to it. 4) Keep browser requests CORS-'simple' (GET with query in URL, or POST with a URLSearchParams body and no custom headers such as Api-User-Agent) so no OPTIONS preflight is needed; Blazegraph's handling of preflight OPTIONS was not verified. Responses carry `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300`, so identical GETs may be served from the CDN for 5 minutes. 5) Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is only emitted on non-OAuth clusters (wdqs main/scholarly/test: oauth=false); the OAuth variant (Commons Query Service) echoes the Origin with credentials instead.

sources.name: National Park Service — National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) ArcGIS REST (points + district polygons)
sources.example_request: Listed properties within a ~1 km box around the address (envelope query, the pattern proven in browser code): https://mapservices.nps.gov/arcgis/rest/services/cultural_resources/nrhp_locations/MapServer/0/query?geometry=-77.047,38.891,-77.026,38.904&geometryType=esriGeometryEnvelope&inSR=4326&spatialRel=esriSpatialRelIntersects&outFields=RESNAME,ResType,Address,City,County,State,NRIS_Refnum,Is_NHL&returnGeometry=true&outSR=4326&f=geojson  |  Which historic district(s) contain the address (point-in-polygon): https://mapservices.nps.gov/arcgis/rest/services/cultural_resources/nrhp_locations/MapServer/1/query?geometry=-77.0365,38.8977&geometryType=esriGeometryPoint&inSR=4326&spatialRel=esriSpatialRelIntersects&outFields=RESNAME,ResType,NRIS_Refnum,City,County,State&returnGeometry=false&f=json  |  (ArcGIS Server >=10.3 also accepts &distance=800&units=esriSRUnit_Meter with a point geometry instead of an envelope)
sources.what_it_gives: All public, non-restricted NRHP listings (~95k+ properties: buildings, sites, structures, objects, districts) as points (layer 0) and polygons (layer 1), with RESNAME, ResType, Address, City, County, State, NRIS_Refnum (reference number, links to the nomination PDF at https://npgallery.nps.gov/AssetDetail/NRIS/<refnum> and catalog.archives.gov), Is_NHL, IS_EXTANT. Output f=json or f=geojson or pbf; maxRecordCount 2000; supports where=, envelope/point/polygon geometry filters, statistics. Tells you if the house/block is itself listed or sits inside a historic district, and gives the registered historic name to feed into the LoC and Internet Archive text searches.
sources.ring_or_timescale: house/lot (listed building), block/street (historic district polygons), neighborhood, city, county (listing counts); the records describe periods of significance from the 1600s to the 1970s, listing dates 1966-present
evidence_urls: https://github.com/jbranigan/neighborhood-history-map/blob/master/js/map.js (static site, $.getJSON to the NPS /MapServer/0/query with geometry= envelope, f=json, no proxy)
sources.license_attribution: US federal government work (NPS), public domain; data.gov lists it as open. Courtesy credit 'National Park Service, National Register of Historic Places'. Sensitive/restricted archaeological sites are already excluded from the public layers.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: No published numeric rate limit; ArcGIS Server caps responses at maxRecordCount=2000 per query (use resultOffset for paging, or small envelopes). Keep outFields minimal and returnGeometry=false for district lookups. Expect occasional slowness; cache per address.
sources.notes: CORS inferred, not live-tested (mapservices.nps.gov blocked here): ArcGIS Server ships with CORS '*' enabled by default, and the cited static-site project calls this exact layer from the browser. A hosted ArcGIS Online copy exists under the NPS open-data hub (item 18fe4b262473496a8ca7871a67d844ee) and AGOL hosted FeatureServers are also CORS-enabled; use it as a fallback if the on-prem server is down. UK equivalent, same ArcGIS REST pattern and license-friendly: Historic England National Heritage List for England FeatureServer (listed buildings, scheduled monuments, parks, battlefields), Open Government Licence v3, https://services-eu1.arcgis.com/ZOdPfBS3aqqDYPUQ/ArcGIS/rest/services/National_Heritage_List_for_England_NHLE_v02_VIEW/FeatureServer (data in EPSG:27700; pass inSR=4326&outSR=4326). Date fields (listing date / period of significance) were not confirmed in the NPS layer schema; read the layer page's fields list once network access is available.

votes.reasoning: Could not reach mapservices.nps.gov, nps.gov, data.gov, arcgis.com or Esri docs from the sandbox (egress-blocked), and the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so all evidence is from GitHub source code (raw.githubusercontent.com + GitHub code search). EXISTENCE: strongly supported and recent. 74 GitHub files reference exactly https://mapservices.nps.gov/arcgis/rest/services/cultural_resources/nrhp_locations/MapServer, 25 of them layer 1. Dated live-use evidence: sulmusic2-star/groundtruth-geo evidence records (retrieved_at 2026-08-20) store a layer-1 point-in-polygon query (geometry=lon,lat&geometryType=esriGeometryPoint&inSR=4326&spatialRel=esriSpatialRelIntersects&returnGeometry=false&f=json) that returned 1 feature with the real schema (NRIS_Refnum, RESNAME, ResType, Address, City, State, CertDate '04/11/72', CR_ID, PROPERTY_ID, STATUS 'Listed', NARA_URL, EDIT_DATE/SRC_DATE as esriFieldTypeDate); goedelsoup/allen-county-ohio catalog (retrieved 2026-08-31) documents both layer 0 and layer 1 queries with where=State='OHIO' AND County='Allen' and the 2,000 record cap; mikedlabs/frederick-radius historicSites.ts says 'keyless ArcGIS REST services ... Verified live 2026-06-20 (... 50 register points)' plus a 2026-07-20 discovery doc; the actively-run alltheplaces spider (locations/spiders/government/national_register_of_historic_places.py) scrapes layer 0 with STATUS='Listed', and its base class first reads the layer's supportedQueryFormats and requires geoJSON, then pages with resultOffset/resultRecordCount and f=geojson, so geoJSON output and maxRecordCount paging are confirmed for layer 0; pnnl/nepa-mcp (a national-lab project) queries both layers with outFields NRIS_Refnum,RESNAME,ResType,Address,City,County,State,CertDate,Is_NHL,STATUS,NARA_URL,IS_EXTANT. Chronicarum (layer 0, full dump) and pre-car-homes, schubert-livability-scout, kingston-historic-data, Ares-Farms, rwspatial/everything (layer 1) all use the same path. API KEY: every caller found sends no token; frederick-radius and pnnl's license table explicitly call it keyless. CORS: no direct Access-Control-Allow-Origin header capture was found anywhere on GitHub, so this remains inferred, but from several independent browser-side callers to this exact service, not just one: jbranigan/neighborhood-history-map (static site, $.getJSON with no callback= param, i.e. a CORS XHR, to MapServer/0/query); mayaomiller/MAP673-Final index.html (a static Leaflet page using L.esri.identifyFeatures against this MapServer and a bare browser fetch() of .../nrhp_locations/MapServer/legend?f=pjson); onaxyzogden/atlas apps/web/src/lib/layerFetcher.ts (a front-end module with localStorage caching that fetch()es MapServer/0/query?...&f=geojson directly, no proxy; its only proxied source is NRCan HRDEM). In addition, ArcGIS JS API 4.x FeatureLayer pages (Connor-04/BearA-Where-Midterm-Popp, vcj/apostleislands) load other services on the same host, and that API has no JSONP/proxy fallback, while ArcGIS Server CORS allowed-origins is a server-wide setting. Combined with ArcGIS Server's default of allowing all origins, cors=yes is credible but still unverified by header. Side claims not verified: no usage of distance=/units=esriSRUnit_Meter or f=pbf against this layer was found (every caller uses envelope/point geometry or where= with f=json or f=geojson); the server version is unknown, so treat pbf and buffered-point queries as untested. The claim's record count and the 'listings only' characterization are inaccurate (see corrected_facts).
votes.corrected_facts: 1) Record count: the service publishes roughly 89,500 records, not '~95k+': about 70,500 Listed points in layer 0 (Chronicarum counted 72,668 points including non-Listed) plus 19,405 polygons in layer 1, with only ~451 listings appearing in both layers (alltheplaces spider comment). The ~95,000 figure is the total NRHP including withheld/restricted sites that are absent from these public layers. 2) The two layers are largely disjoint, not two representations of the same set: a property is mapped as a point OR a polygon, and layer 1 holds not only districts but also NHLs and other large properties (e.g. SF Cable Cars NHL 66000233 is only in layer 1), so a 'what is listed near this address' search must union layer 0 and layer 1; querying points alone silently drops districts and many landmarks. 3) Layer 0/1 are not 'listings only': STATUS is 'Listed', 'Removed' or null; filter where=STATUS='Listed' to exclude delisted/demolished properties. 4) Date fields exist: CertDate (listing/certification date, a string like '04/11/72' or '1966-10-15' depending on format), plus EDIT_DATE and SRC_DATE (esriFieldTypeDate, epoch ms). Other useful fields: NARA_URL (direct link to the nomination scan), CR_ID, PROPERTY_ID, GEOM_ID (the unique id; NRIS_Refnum collides for ~1,500 layer-0 points because one listing can be mapped as several points), NumCBldg etc. (contributing-resource counts), MultiName, BND_TYPE, MAP_METHOD, SRC_ACCU. 5) State values are spelled-out upper-case names (State='MARYLAND'), not postal codes; Is_NHL is 'X' when set; IS_EXTANT is 'Unknown' for batch-created rows. 6) Point positions are mostly 'Arbitrary point'/centroid-derived with a stated ±12 m accuracy and observed ~30 m error, so a point tells you the block, not the parcel; use the layer-1 polygon for 'is this lot inside a district'. 7) f=geojson is confirmed in use (alltheplaces checks supportedQueryFormats contains geoJSON); f=pbf and the distance/units buffered-point query are unverified for this server. 8) CORS is inferred from multiple static-site/browser callers, not from an observed Access-Control-Allow-Origin header; live-verify once network access is available.

sources.name: Internet Archive advancedsearch (metadata search over texts, images, maps; county/city histories, photo collections)
sources.example_request: https://archive.org/advancedsearch.php?q=%28%22Pennsylvania+Avenue%22+OR+%22Lafayette+Square%22%29+AND+Washington+AND+mediatype%3A%28texts+OR+image%29&fl%5B%5D=identifier&fl%5B%5D=title&fl%5B%5D=date&fl%5B%5D=mediatype&fl%5B%5D=description&fl%5B%5D=subject&sort%5B%5D=date+asc&rows=50&page=1&output=json | County/city histories for the county ring: https://archive.org/advancedsearch.php?q=title%3A%28%22history+of%22+AND+%22District+of+Columbia%22%29+AND+mediatype%3Atexts&fl%5B%5D=identifier&fl%5B%5D=title&fl%5B%5D=date&fl%5B%5D=creator&sort%5B%5D=date+asc&rows=30&output=json (thumbnail for display: https://archive.org/services/img/{identifier} as an ; item page https://archive.org/details/{identifier}; full-text reader at /details/{identifier}?q=)
sources.what_it_gives: Lucene-style metadata search across ~tens of millions of items: digitized 19th/20th-century county and town histories, city directories, atlases and plat books, photo collections, Sanborn-style maps, yearbooks, newspapers not in LoC. Returns identifier, title, date, creator, description, subject, mediatype, collection; numFound for counts (rows=0). No geo field, so you search by the place names from the reverse geocode (street, neighborhood, city, county) and by the NRHP historic name. Pair with the Wayback 'available' API (https://archive.org/wayback/available?url=...&timestamp=YYYYMMDD, also CORS *) to show what a local website looked like in a given year.
sources.ring_or_timescale: street, neighborhood, city, county, state (text search on place names); decades from the 1600s to the 20th century (historical texts) and 1996-present (Wayback for web history)
evidence_urls: https://github.com/fuzheado/Internet-Archive-AI-Skills/blob/main/.claude/skills/internet-archive-api/SKILL.md (CORS matrix: advancedsearch.php and services/search/v1/scrape and wayback/available return Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *; services/img and download nodes do not)
sources.license_attribution: No key for read-only search. Metadata is freely reusable; each item's content carries its own rights (most pre-1930 texts and government material are public domain; check the 'licenseurl'/'rights' fields and link to the item page). IA asks for a link back and reasonable load.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: No numeric limits published; IA documents a qualitative contract: honor 429 + Retry-After, keep concurrency low, cache responses, prefer rows-limited queries; community experience is that >=1 request/second per client is safe. Count-only via rows=0. The scrape API (services/search/v1/scrape, cursor-based) is for bulk and also CORS-enabled. Thumbnails via services/img are -only (no CORS header), fine for display, not for canvas pixel reads (use IIIF: https://iiif.archive.org/iiif/{id}$0/full/400,/0/default.jpg).
sources.notes: Not live-tested here. Quality depends on crafting queries from place names; use the NRHP RESNAME, the street name, the neighborhood and the county name as separate queries and merge by date. The IA full-text search backend (be-api.us.archive.org/fts) is undocumented and its CORS behaviour is unverified, so stick to advancedsearch metadata search.

sources.name: Pleiades gazetteer of ancient places (per-place JSON from pleiades.stoa.org + CC-BY dataset dumps / GitHub GeoJSON mirror for geo lookup)
sources.base_url: https://pleiades.stoa.org/places/{pid}/json  (per place; CORS)  +  https://github.com/isawnyu/pleiades.datasets/releases (places.csv / per-place JSON, CC BY 3.0) or https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ryanfb/pleiades-geojson/gh-pages/geojson/{pid}.geojson and .../name_index.json
sources.example_request: For lat=38.8977 lon=-77.0365 Pleiades returns nothing (its scope is the ancient Mediterranean/Old World, roughly 3000 BCE-700 CE), so the UI should show 'no ancient gazetteer coverage here'. For a European address, e.g. 51.5074,-0.1278, a bundled index built from places.csv (columns include representative latitude/longitude, bounding_box_wkt, time periods, min/max dates, feature types) finds Londinium (pid 79574), then: https://pleiades.stoa.org/places/79574/json  -> GeoJSON FeatureCollection with title, description, names[], reprPoint, bbox, locations[] (each with geometry, start/end years, accuracy), connectsWith[], placeTypes[], references[].  Static mirror alternative (no origin server load): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ryanfb/pleiades-geojson/gh-pages/geojson/79574.geojson and the name->pid list https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ryanfb/pleiades-geojson/gh-pages/name_index.json
sources.what_it_gives: ~40,000 ancient places (cities, forts, roads, rivers, regions, peoples) with representative coordinates, bounding boxes, attested ancient and modern names, dated locations with time-period keys (archaic, classical, hellenistic, roman, late antique ...), connections to other places, and scholarly references. Gives the 'what was here in antiquity' text for the city/region rings and date ranges per place for the millennia end of the slider.
sources.ring_or_timescale: neighborhood (site-level, accuracy radius given), city, county/region, country/province (ancient regions); centuries and millennia, roughly 3000 BCE to 700 CE (some medieval); Old World only (Europe, N. Africa, Near East, Central/South Asia, China partially)
evidence_urls: https://github.com/isawnyu/pleiades.datasets (README: CC BY 3.0; data/json/ per-place files; data/gis/places.csv; release 4.1, May 2025)
https://github.com/ryanfb/pleiades-geojson (gh-pages branch holds geojson/{pid}.geojson + name_index.json, CC-BY data; verified readable via raw.githubusercontent.com in this session)

https://github.com/isawnyu/pleiades_search_api (shows the only server-side search is https://pleiades.stoa.org/search_rss?... returning RSS/XML, params SearchableText, Subject:list, portal_type:list=Place, getFeatureType, bbox)
https://api.pleiades.stoa.org/ (legacy 'Pleiades Places API' page: 'read-only JSON over HTTP, supports CORS but not JSONP')
sources.license_attribution: Data: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 (CC-BY) — you must credit 'Pleiades (pleiades.stoa.org), Ancient World Mapping Center / ISAW NYU' and link the place URI. Code in the mirror repo is MIT. No key.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: No published limits; the official Python client sets a descriptive User-Agent and caches aggressively, and community scripts throttle to ~1 request/second. Per-place JSON is tiny and cacheable (Expires headers are set). For geo search do NOT hit the live site: build a compact index (pid, title, lat, lon, minDate, maxDate, placeTypes) from a numbered dataset release at build time (places.csv is a few MB; a trimmed JSON index is ~1-2 MB) and ship it with the site, then fetch the per-place JSON on demand.
sources.notes: Live per-place fetch not testable here (pleiades.stoa.org blocked by proxy); CORS evidence is a browser-side fetch in a third-party static JS file plus the 2011-era API page statement. The /search_rss endpoint is XML and its CORS status is unverified, so treat the live server as per-place-detail only. The raw.githubusercontent.com mirror was actually fetched in this session (200, valid GeoJSON for pid 579885 Athenae), but it is a 2014-era script output and may lag the current dataset; prefer generating your own index from the 2025 release and hosting it on your GitHub Pages origin (same-origin, no CORS at all).

sources.name: Native Land Digital API — Indigenous territories, languages, treaties at a point
sources.example_request: https://native-land.ca/api/index.php?maps=territories,languages,treaties&position=38.8977,-77.0365&key=YOUR_FREE_KEY  -> JSON array of GeoJSON Features; each feature.properties has Name (e.g. 'Piscataway', 'Nacotchtank (Anacostan)'), Slug, description (link to the nation's page on native-land.ca), color, and the polygon geometry. Full polygon layers for a bundled/offline map: https://native-land.ca/api/polygons/geojson/territories?key=YOUR_FREE_KEY (also .../languages, .../treaties). Other query modes: ?maps=territories&name=<slug>, and by intersecting polygon.
sources.what_it_gives: The overlapping Indigenous territory polygons, language areas and treaty areas for any coordinate worldwide (strongest in North America, Australia/NZ, growing elsewhere), with names, colors, polygon geometry and a link to each nation's description. This is the only widely used source for the 'before colonial records' layer of the house -> country rings and for the pre-1600s part of the time slider.
sources.ring_or_timescale: house through region/state (territory polygons are large, so one answer covers all inner rings); timescale: pre-contact to present (NLD explicitly does not date its polygons; treat as 'traditional territory, ongoing'; treaty layer carries treaty years in its names/descriptions)
evidence_urls: https://github.com/native-land-digital/next-nld/blob/main/src/components/ai/chatbot/MessageParser.js ('use client' React component that fetches https://native-land.ca/api/index.php?maps=territories&position=lat,lng&key=... directly from the visitor's browser)
https://github.com/hyphacoop/countermapland (SvelteKit client calling the same endpoint from the browser)
sources.license_attribution: Since late 2024 every request needs an API key: create a free account at native-land.ca, open the API tab, tick the box to accept the Indigenous Data Sovereignty Treaty. Treaty terms (as summarized by their docs): educational/research and non-commercial use only; no monetized platforms, resale, bundling or charging for access; must attribute Native Land Digital as the source and acknowledge Indigenous communities as stewards; must not alter or misrepresent territories; NLD may revoke keys for misuse. A free, non-commercial hobby site fits; add a visible 'Data: Native Land Digital (native-land.ca)' credit and their disclaimer that boundaries are not authoritative/legal.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: No numeric limits found (docs site was unreachable from this sandbox; their 2024 announcement says the key exists 'to keep a better handle on excessive requests'). Because the key is required and the call must come from the browser, the key will be visible in your page source — this is exactly what NLD's own front end does, but it means abuse could get your key revoked; cache results per address in localStorage and avoid calling on every map move. The full-GeoJSON endpoint returns multi-MB files: if you bundle a snapshot, keep attribution and re-check the treaty text for redistribution wording before doing so.
sources.notes: The old keyless endpoint (still seen in many GitHub projects) now returns an error without key=. Terms shifted from 'completely open' to key-gated non-commercial in late 2024; re-read https://api-docs.native-land.ca/data-sovereignty-treaty and about-and-disclaimers before launch, and consider a toggle so the layer degrades gracefully if the key is revoked.

gaps: 1) Year built for an arbitrary US address: no free, keyless, nationwide source exists. OSM start_date has ~14.2 million objects globally but is concentrated in bulk-import countries (Netherlands BAG, Denmark, Czech RÚIAN); US building coverage is sparse, so treat it as a bonus when present (Overpass: https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter?data=[out:json][timeout:25];(way(around:40,38.8977,-77.0365)[building][start_date];way(around:300,38.8977,-77.0365)[highway][\"name:etymology:wikidata\"];);out tags center; — Overpass adds Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * when an Origin header is sent, no key, usage policy ~10,000 queries and 1 GB per day per IP for one-off use, 'divide by 100' for a regularly running app, returns 429/406 when over; note overpass-api.de returns 406 with no CORS header to private-LAN origins, so develop on localhost/127.0.0.1 or a deployed preview). County assessor/parcel data with year_built is per-jurisdiction: Socrata SODA portals (NYC PLUTO, SF assessor roll, Cook County, Seattle; CORS yes, app token optional) and Carto SQL (Philadelphia OPA) each need a dataset-specific adapter; nationwide aggregators (Regrid, ATTOM, Realie, Apify scrapers) are paid. Judgment: not general; ship OSM start_date + NRHP, and optionally a small per-city plugin table for 3-5 big cities. 2) Street name origins: Wikidata P138 and OSM name:etymology:wikidata are rich in parts of Europe and thin in the US; expect 'unknown' for most American streets. 3) Key-required second tier (all free keys, all usable from the browser but the key is exposed in page source): DPLA https://api.dp.la/v2/items?sourceResource.spatial.coordinates=38.8977,-77.0365&sourceResource.spatial.distance=5mi&page_size=50&api_key=KEY (free instant key via POST https://api.dp.la/v2/api_key/you@example.com; policy says no rate limiting in general; a 2017 captured response shows Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * but this is old evidence); Europeana https://api.europeana.eu/record/v2/search.json?query=*&qf=distance(coverageLocation,51.5074,-0.1278,5)&sort=distance+asc&rows=50&wskey=KEY (free key, header X-Api-Key preferred over wskey; Europeana documents CORS for all its APIs; fair-use policy with no fixed numbers; Europe-focused); Smithsonian Open Access https://api.si.edu/openaccess/api/v1.0/search?q=%22Washington+(D.C.)%22+AND+online_media_type:Images&rows=20&api_key=DEMO_KEY (key from api.data.gov: DEMO_KEY 30 req/hour and 50/day per IP, registered keys 1,000/hour; CC0 metadata/images; a static-site provider script on GitHub calls it from the browser with DEMO_KEY, so CORS appears to work but is unverified; no lat/lon search, text place names only); Flickr Commons (flickr.photos.search with lat/lon/radius and is_commons=true; key required, CORS from api.flickr.com not confirmed, skip). 4) Chronicling America stops at 1963 and HABS/NRHP only cover documented/listed buildings; an ordinary 1970s house will have no house-level records in any of these — the house ring must fall back to block/street context. 5) Nothing here dates Indigenous territory polygons; NLD is a present-day/traditional map, not a time series. 6) None of these were live-tested from this sandbox (egress blocked); CORS claims rest on documentation and on public browser-side code that calls each endpoint without a proxy.
recommendation: Build the human-history rings on four keyless, CORS-friendly services first, in this order: (1) Wikidata SPARQL around-query (P625 + P585/P571) — one request yields a dated, geolocated event/construction timeline for every ring and drives the slider from years to millennia; (2) loc.gov JSON API — Chronicling America (street/neighborhood/city newspapers by year range, with OCR text) and HABS/HAER/HALS + photos/maps via fa=location:<city>, the richest free US house-to-city layer; (3) NPS NRHP ArcGIS REST — point-in-polygon tells whether the address sits in a historic district and lists registered buildings on the block, and its RESNAME feeds better text queries into (2) and (4); (4) Internet Archive advancedsearch — county/town histories and photo collections for the county/state rings, plus Wayback for recent web history. Add Pleiades as a bundled index (CC-BY, built from the 2025 dataset release, hosted on your own Pages origin) with live per-place JSON for the ancient end of the slider, Old World only. Add Native Land Digital last, behind a free key and clear attribution, since it is the only source for the pre-colonial layer but its key must sit in client code and its terms are non-commercial only. Keep DPLA/Europeana/Smithsonian as optional 'more images' plugins gated on the visitor (or you) supplying a key. For year-built, show OSM start_date and NRHP when present and say honestly when unknown.

sources.name: GitHub Pages (static hosting)
sources.example_request: curl -sI -H 'Origin: https://example.org' https://<user>.github.io/<repo>/data/geology.json | grep -i -E 'access-control|accept-ranges|cache-control'  (expect: access-control-allow-origin: * ; accept-ranges: bytes)
sources.what_it_gives: Free HTTPS hosting for the built Vite site plus any static data files we ship ourselves (JSON, GeoJSON, PMTiles). Served files carry Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and support HTTP Range requests, so our own data is usable cross-origin and PMTiles archives can be range-read without a tile server.
sources.ring_or_timescale: Infrastructure for all rings and time scales; especially the deep-time rings (continent/plate, eons) whose data we can pre-bake and ship as static files inside the 1 GB site limit.
sources.license_attribution: GitHub Terms of Service; Pages may not be used as commercial hosting / SaaS (hobby site is fine). No sensitive data.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: Official limits (docs source read from github/docs repo): published site <= 1 GB; source repo recommended <= 1 GB; deployments time out after 10 minutes; SOFT bandwidth limit 100 GB/month; SOFT limit of 10 builds/hour which does NOT apply when publishing with a custom Actions workflow; Pages itself may return HTTP 429 under its own rate limiting; one user/org site per account (project sites unlimited). Pages is available for PUBLIC repos on GitHub Free; private-repo Pages needs Pro/Team. Pages sites are always public on the internet even from a private repo. GitHub Actions minutes are free for public repos.
sources.notes: Hard constraints that shape the design: (1) HTTPS is enforced on *.github.io, so any data source reachable only over http:// is unusable from the page (mixed-content block, surfaces as a NetworkError even when CORS would be fine). (2) You cannot set custom response headers (no Cache-Control, CSP, COOP/COEP) and there are no server-side redirects/rewrites; everything must be client side. Reported default caching is a short max-age (~10 min) for HTML, which is fine because Vite emits content-hashed asset filenames. (3) Project sites live under a path prefix, so Vite needs base: '/<repo>/' (or pass configure-pages' base_path output to `vite build --base`), and MapLibre worker/CSS URLs must resolve under that base. (4) IMPORTANT storage gotcha: the web origin is https://<user>.github.io for ALL of that user's project sites, so localStorage/IndexedDB/Cache API names are shared with every other project page the owner hosts; prefix all keys and cache names (e.g. 'sno-ball:v1:') and register any service worker with scope '/<repo>/'. (5) No SPA path routing: encode state in the query/hash (?q=<address>&t=1900) so deep links work without a 404.html hack. (6) Pages serves with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * for public sites (community discussions confirm; cannot be changed), which is what lets a Cloudflare Worker, another site, or a dev server fetch our data bundles. (7) Range requests work, so a PMTiles archive (pmtiles npm 4.5.0) of pre-rendered historical/geologic layers can be hosted in the repo if < 1 GB total; Protomaps' own docs list GitHub Pages as an easy host when the file fits. Bandwidth math: at 100 GB/month soft limit a hobby site with a 2 MB first load supports ~50k visits/month; keep heavy rasters out of the repo or behind on-demand fetches.

THE 'enablement' INPUT, EXPLAINED: configure-pages first calls GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pages. If Pages is not enabled that call fails; with enablement=false (the default) the action errors with 'Get Pages site failed. Please verify that the repository has Pages enabled and configured to build using GitHub Actions, or consider exploring the `enablement` parameter'. With enablement: true it instead calls POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pages with build_type: 'workflow' (idempotent: a 409 'already exists' is swallowed). BUT action.yml states this requires a token other than GITHUB_TOKEN (a PAT with repo scope / Pages write, or a GitHub App with administration:write + pages:write) because GITHUB_TOKEN cannot create a Pages site; so for a beginner the realistic path is the ONE-TIME MANUAL STEP: repo Settings -> Pages -> Build and deployment -> Source -> 'GitHub Actions' (docs source: configuring-a-publishing-source). Alternative one-liner from the owner's machine with gh logged in: `gh api -X POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/pages -f build_type=workflow`. Do NOT add a PAT secret just for enablement; leave enablement unset.

RECOMMENDED WORKFLOW (two jobs, matches docs):
name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write
concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: { node-version: lts/*, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run typecheck && npm test
      - id: pages
        uses: actions/configure-pages@v6
      - run: npm run build -- --base "${{ steps.pages.outputs.base_path }}/"
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with: { path: ./dist }
  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5

configure-pages outputs base_url/origin/host/base_path and sets GITHUB_PAGES=true; feeding base_path to Vite avoids hard-coding the repo name. For PR checks add a separate job that runs `npx playwright install --with-deps chromium` then `npx playwright test` against `vite preview` (Playwright CI docs). lts/* resolves to Node 24, which satisfies Vite 8 (^20.19||>=22.12) and Vitest 5 (^22.12||^24||>=26). Pin to SHAs later if desired (Vite's sample shows the SHAs for the v7/v7/v6/v5/v5 set).

sources.name: Browser CORS model and exact failure modes (MDN)
sources.example_request: fetch('https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/reverse?lat=38.8977&lon=-77.0365&format=jsonv2&zoom=18', { method: 'GET', mode: 'cors', credentials: 'omit' })  // keep it a 'simple' request: GET, no custom headers
sources.what_it_gives: The rules that decide whether a data source is usable at all from a GitHub Pages page, and what each failure looks like to our JavaScript so the app can react correctly instead of guessing.
sources.ring_or_timescale: Applies to every remote ring/time source.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: n/a
sources.notes: FAILURE MODES, each with how it surfaces in code: (1) Response lacks Access-Control-Allow-Origin -> fetch() REJECTS with TypeError ('Failed to fetch' in Chrome, 'NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource.' in Firefox). Status code and body are unreadable; only the DevTools console shows the CORS reason. Code cannot distinguish this from offline/DNS failure. (2) Server adds CORS headers only on 200s but not on 403/429/5xx -> the SAME TypeError, so you never see the 429 or its Retry-After; treat TypeError from a known-CORS host as 'back off with jitter', not 'host is down'. (3) Even on a CORS-OK 429, response.headers.get('Retry-After') returns null unless the server sends Access-Control-Expose-Headers: Retry-After (only Cache-Control, Content-Language, Content-Length, Content-Type, Expires, Last-Modified, Pragma are safelisted) -> implement client-side backoff that does not depend on Retry-After. (4) Preflight: anything beyond GET/HEAD/POST with safelisted headers and form/text content types triggers an OPTIONS request that the server must answer 2xx with ACAO/ACAM/ACAH; many static/legacy servers 405 it. Keep every call 'simple': GET with query params, or POST with application/x-www-form-urlencoded (Overpass style); never add Authorization/X-Requested-With/Content-Type: application/json unless the host documents CORS preflight support. (5) credentials: 'include' with ACAO: * is rejected; always use credentials: 'omit'. (6) mode: 'no-cors' returns an opaque response (status 0, body unreadable) - useless for JSON and, if stored in the Cache API, Chrome pads each opaque entry to ~7 MB of quota. (7) A redirect to a host without CORS fails like (1). (8) Mixed content: an http:// endpoint is blocked outright from the https:// Pages origin. (9) MapLibre loads tiles/sprites/glyphs with fetch, so tile and style hosts need CORS too (an would display but cannot feed WebGL). (10) User-Agent cannot be relied on from browser fetch (forbidden/dropped by Chrome per MDN), so policies that require identifying the app must be satisfied via the Referer header, which browsers send automatically; under the default referrer policy (strict-origin-when-cross-origin) a cross-origin HTTPS->HTTPS request carries only the origin (https://.github.io/). Never set referrerPolicy: 'no-referrer' or a , or the site loses its identity to Nominatim-style policies. DIAGNOSIS (once network is open): curl -sI -H 'Origin: https://.github.io' '' | grep -i access-control; then repeat for an error path to see whether 4xx/5xx also carry the header.

sources.name: Public Nominatim as a browser-direct client (worked CORS/rate-limit example, verified from OSMF infrastructure code)
sources.example_request: https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/reverse?lat=38.8977&lon=-77.0365&format=jsonv2&zoom=18&addressdetails=1   (and /search?q=<address>&format=jsonv2&limit=5&addressdetails=1 on explicit submit only)
sources.what_it_gives: The canonical example of how a free OSM-run API behaves for browser JS: permissive CORS is on by default in Nominatim (NOMINATIM_CORS_NOACCESSCONTROL=yes), the OSMF nginx front answers OPTIONS preflights with ACAO:* and (unusually) also puts Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * `always` on its 403 and 429/503 error pages, so error statuses ARE readable from JS; requests are blocked (403) when they carry no email, no Referer AND an empty User-Agent, or match private blocklists.
sources.ring_or_timescale: House/lot -> block -> street -> neighborhood -> city rings (present-day address resolution); not a time source.
sources.license_attribution: Data (c) OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL; show attribution in the UI.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: OSMF usage policy: absolute maximum 1 request/second; provide a valid HTTP Referer or User-Agent identifying the application (a browser page satisfies this through Referer); NO auto-complete/type-ahead; bulk geocoding discouraged (single thread, ~4 req/min for long-running jobs); results must be cached on your side; periodic app requests count as bulk; 'if at all possible set up a proxy and enable caching'. nginx: `keepalive_requests 2`, fail2ban on nginx limit_req, private blocklists for user agents/referrers/emails. Note: the live rule `map $missing_email$missing_referer$http_user_agent ... "11" -> blocked` only fires when there is no email param, no Referer and an EMPTY UA, so a normal browser request with Referer passes that gate.
sources.notes: Design consequences for the app: address lookup must be an explicit action (Enter/button), never per-keystroke; one Nominatim request at a time with >= 1.1 s spacing (p-queue concurrency 1, interval 1100, intervalCap 1, strict true); cache geocode results in IndexedDB for weeks (policy requires caching); add &email= only if you want a contact identifier (it appears in server logs; optional). The 'ACAO only with Referer' claim in older discussions is not what the current chef config shows, but it is harmless to simply keep the default referrer policy. Nominatim's own web UI (nominatim-ui) is a static page that calls the API from the browser, which is the documentary proof that browser-direct use works. Live verification pending (sandbox returns 403 from the egress proxy).

sources.name: Cloudflare Workers free tier as an optional CORS/caching proxy
sources.example_request: https://sno-ball-proxy.<subdomain>.workers.dev/?u=https%3A%2F%2Fnominatim.openstreetmap.org%2Freverse%3Flat%3D38.8977%26lon%3D-77.0365%26format%3Djsonv2  (worker allowlists upstream hosts, adds User-Agent 'sno-ball/1.0 (contact@example.com)', caches with caches.default, returns ACAO: https://<user>.github.io)
sources.what_it_gives: A zero-cost escape hatch for any source that lacks CORS, needs a server-set User-Agent, or benefits from shared caching across all visitors. Not required for the baseline product, but the cheapest way to add a non-CORS source later.
sources.ring_or_timescale: Infrastructure; useful for any ring whose best source lacks CORS.
sources.license_attribution: Cloudflare terms; free plan permits commercial use.
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: Workers Free (from limits.mdx): 100,000 requests/day resetting at 00:00 UTC (exceeding returns Error 1027; worker can be configured fail-open = bypass or fail-closed = 1027 page); 10 ms CPU time per request; 128 MB memory; 50 subrequests per invocation (1,000 to internal services); burst limit 1,000 requests/minute; 100 MB script size budget; Cache API calls count against the subrequest quota. No credit card required; workers.dev subdomain provided.
sources.notes: WHAT A BEGINNER OWNER WOULD NEED: (1) a Cloudflare account (email + password, no card); (2) in the dashboard: Workers & Pages -> Create -> Create Worker -> Deploy, then 'Edit code' and paste a ~40-line proxy (the official cors-header-proxy example shows the pattern: read target URL from a query param, forward, copy response, set Access-Control-Allow-Origin and Vary: Origin, answer OPTIONS); (3) nothing else - a pure proxy for keyless APIs needs NO secrets. If a key were ever needed it goes in Settings -> Variables and Secrets -> Add -> Secret (or `wrangler secret put NAME` from a terminal), never in the GitHub repo. The CLI path (Node + `npx wrangler deploy`, or the cloudflare/wrangler-action in GitHub Actions with an API token secret) is optional. HARD RULES for the proxy: allowlist upstream hostnames (never an open proxy), restrict ACAO to the Pages origin, forward only GET, set a real User-Agent with contact info (satisfies Nominatim/Wikimedia-style policies that browsers cannot), cache with caches.default or Cache-Control so repeated lookups never reach the upstream, and add a per-IP throttle if abuse appears. Budget: 100k/day is ample for a hobby site but a single abusive client could exhaust it, so prefer fail-open semantics only for non-critical paths and keep the site working without the proxy. Trade-off: adds a second account and a dependency the owner must keep alive; recommend shipping WITHOUT it and adding only if a specific source proves non-CORS.

Netlify Free: 100 GB bandwidth, 300 build minutes, 125k function invocations + 1M edge function invocations per month, no card.

Compared with Cloudflare Workers: more generous invocation counts on Vercel, but a function cold start and a full project per proxy; Workers' dashboard-paste flow is simpler for a one-file proxy. Recommendation: if a proxy is ever needed, use Cloudflare Workers; keep Vercel/Netlify as fallbacks.

sources.name: Client-side caching stack (Cache API, IndexedDB, localStorage, StorageManager)
sources.example_request: const key = 'sno-ball:v1:nominatim:reverse:38.89770,-77.03650'; const hit = await idbGet(key); if (hit && Date.now() - hit.fetchedAt < hit.ttlMs) return hit.body; ... await idbSet(key, { fetchedAt: Date.now(), ttlMs: 30*864e5, body });
sources.what_it_gives: Durable per-visitor memoization so repeated/revisited lookups never re-hit free APIs, plus offline-ish resilience; the component that makes 'respectful' use achievable.
sources.ring_or_timescale: All rings; TTLs vary by ring (present-day geocode/OSM data days-weeks; historical/geologic data effectively immutable).
sources.license_attribution: Caching API results is permitted/required by Nominatim's policy; keep attribution with cached data. Check each data source's terms for caching limits (other subagents).
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: Quotas (web.dev / 2026 summaries): origin quota shared by IndexedDB + Cache API + service-worker storage; Chrome/Edge up to ~60% of disk per origin, Firefox ~10% (more with persist()), Safari large in-browser; navigator.storage.estimate() reports usage/quota (excludes localStorage); storage is best-effort unless navigator.storage.persist() is granted. localStorage ~5 MB per origin, synchronous, strings only, throws QuotaExceededError. Safari/WebKit ITP deletes ALL script-writable storage (IndexedDB, Cache API, SW) after 7 days of no user interaction with the site (home-screen apps exempt). Cache API is window-accessible on secure contexts (Pages is HTTPS) - no service worker needed. Opaque (no-cors) responses are padded (~7 MB each in Chrome) - never cache them.
sources.notes: RECOMMENDED LAYERS: L0 in-memory Map + in-flight promise dedupe (same URL requested twice while pending shares one fetch). L1 IndexedDB via idb-keyval 6.3.0 (tiny) or idb 8.0.4 for parsed JSON records {fetchedAt, ttlMs, source, body}; TTL per source type (geocode 30 d, Overpass/OSM features 7 d, Wikipedia/Wikidata text 7 d, static deep-time tables = cache forever keyed by app version). L2 browser HTTP cache + Cache API only for our OWN same-origin static bundles (hashed filenames -> safe to keep); do not use Cache API for third-party JSON (no TTL semantics, opaque padding risk). L3 localStorage only for UI prefs and the last ~10 searches. KEY DESIGN: namespace every key/cache name with 'sno-ball:<schemaVersion>:' because the origin https://<user>.github.io is shared with the owner's other project sites; bump schemaVersion to invalidate; canonicalize keys (lower-case trimmed address; lat/lon rounded to 5 decimals ~1 m; sorted query params). Negative caching: store failures for only ~60 s so a flaky source is not hammered but recovers. Sweep expired entries lazily on startup. Show nothing to the user about storage except a 'clear cached data' button. Service worker/Workbox (vite-plugin-pwa 2.0.0, workbox-window 7.4.1) is optional and adds update-flow complexity on Pages; skip in phase 1.

sources.name: Respectful rate limiting: queueing, debouncing, exponential backoff (p-queue, p-retry, AbortController)
sources.example_request: const nominatimQ = new PQueue({ concurrency: 1, interval: 1100, intervalCap: 1, strict: true }); nominatimQ.add(() => pRetry(() => fetchJson(url, { signal }), { retries: 3, factor: 2, minTimeout: 1000, maxTimeout: 15000, randomize: true, shouldRetry: ({error}) => error.name === 'TypeError' || [429,503,502,500].includes(error.status) }))
sources.what_it_gives: Per-host request pacing that keeps the site inside each free API's policy even when many visitors scrub the time slider, plus jittered retries that avoid thundering herds.
sources.ring_or_timescale: All remote sources.
sources.license_attribution: p-queue 9.3.3 and p-retry 8.0.1 are MIT (npm metadata checked 2026-10-07).
sources.rate_limits_and_policy: p-queue: intervalCap (max tasks per interval ms), interval, carryoverConcurrencyCount, and strict: true enforces a sliding window so no more than intervalCap tasks run in ANY rolling interval (recommended by its README for APIs with strict limits). p-retry: retries (default 10 - lower it), factor 2, minTimeout 1000, maxTimeout, randomize: true (full jitter per AWS guidance), shouldRetry(context), signal (AbortSignal), AbortError to stop retrying.
sources.notes: CONCRETE POLICY: one PQueue per upstream host (nominatim: 1/1.1 s; overpass: concurrency 1; wikipedia/wikidata: concurrency 2 with ~250 ms spacing - final numbers from the data-source subagents). Address search runs only on explicit submit (Nominatim bans autocomplete) and dedupes identical queries. Time slider: update local text/era instantly from already-loaded data; schedule network work with a 250-300 ms trailing debounce and cancel superseded work via AbortController (pass signal through p-queue task and fetch); on pointer drag, fetch only on release. Backoff: retry only on TypeError (likely CORS-less 429/5xx), 429, 500/502/503; cap at 3 attempts, full jitter; honor Retry-After when exposed; after N consecutive failures on a host open a 60 s circuit breaker and show 'source busy, using cached data'. Never retry 400/403/404 (policy or bad request). Prefetch nothing speculative beyond the next/previous time step already visible. Log per-host request counts in dev to verify the pacing in Vitest (fake timers).

sources.notes: RECOMMENDATION: start with vanilla TypeScript (Vite 'vanilla-ts' template) plus a ~50-line typed store/event-emitter, for these reasons: (a) MapLibre is imperative, so a VDOM buys little for the map; (b) the UI surface is small and mostly declarative text: address form, ring stack, time slider with scale switcher, narrative panel, attribution strip; (c) a beginner owner maintains fewer concepts (no compiler, no svelte-check/TS version coupling, no JSX config), and the TypeScript 7 transition is simpler without framework type-checkers; (d) smallest bundle and fastest first paint on a bandwidth-capped host. Escape hatch: if the ring/time UI grows beyond ~8 interacting components, adopt Preact 11 (React-compatible API, ~4 KB, via @preact/preset-vite) incrementally, or Svelte 5 for the best size/DX if a rewrite of the UI layer is acceptable; avoid React 19 (10x larger runtime, no benefit here). Structure code as pure modules (time-scale math, cache, queue, ring assembly) tested in Vitest with fake timers, a thin DOM layer, and a map adapter module that is the only file importing maplibre-gl.

gaps: (1) Nothing here was live-verified: the sandbox's egress proxy returns 403 for nominatim, Cloudflare, docs.github.com etc., so every claim rests on source code (OSMF chef nginx template, Nominatim env.defaults, action.yml files, Vite/MapLibre docs in their repos, Cloudflare docs source) and on web-search summaries; the first task once network opens is `curl -sI -H 'Origin: https://<user>.github.io' <url>` against each API for both a 200 path and an error path. (2) The exact GitHub Pages Cache-Control values and the "sends ACAO only with Referer" Nominatim claim come from community/third-party pages, not official docs; treat as plausible, not proven. (3) Vercel/Netlify free-tier numbers are from 2026 third-party round-ups, not fetched official pricing pages. (4) GitHub's `releases` pages could not be scraped, so the "what changed in v6/v5" is inferred from action.yml diffs (node20 -> node24; upload-artifact v4 -> v7) rather than release notes. (5) The architecture cannot make a non-CORS, key-only, or http-only source usable without the optional Cloudflare Worker; which specific sources fall in that bucket is for the data-source subagents. (6) Browser storage is per visitor and evictable (Safari 7-day), so a static site cannot share cached results across visitors; only a proxy with edge caching can. (7) GitHub Pages' 100 GB/month soft limit and the Workers 100k/day limit are adequate for a hobby audience but not for virality; there is no paging/alerting without adding a third-party service.
recommendation: Build it as a plain Vite 8.3 + TypeScript 6.0.3 (not 7.x yet, because typescript-eslint/svelte-check cannot run on 7.0) + maplibre-gl 6.13 vanilla-ts app deployed by the two-job GitHub Actions workflow in the 'GitHub Actions workflow' entry (checkout@v7, setup-node@v7 with lts/*, configure-pages@v6, upload-pages-artifact@v5, deploy-pages@v5; permissions pages: write + id-token: write; environment github-pages; base path from configure-pages' base_path output). The one unavoidable manual step for the owner is Settings -> Pages -> Source -> 'GitHub Actions' (or `gh api -X POST repos/<o>/<r>/pages -f build_type=workflow`); do not use configure-pages' `enablement: true`, which needs a PAT that GITHUB_TOKEN cannot replace. Keep every remote call a CORS 'simple' GET with credentials: 'omit', keep the default referrer policy so the page identifies itself to Nominatim-style policies via Referer, treat fetch TypeErrors from known-CORS hosts as back-off signals (error statuses often lack CORS headers and Retry-After is not exposed), and never use no-cors/opaque responses. Make every lookup go through one cachedFetch() that checks an in-memory map, then IndexedDB (idb-keyval, keys prefixed 'sno-ball:v1:' because <user>.github.io is a shared origin, TTL per source), then a per-host p-queue (Nominatim strictly 1 request/1.1 s, explicit-submit search, no autocomplete) wrapped in p-retry with full jitter and AbortController cancellation; debounce the time slider ~250 ms and fetch on release. Ship the deep-time data (geologic timescale, plate polygons at coarse steps) as static JSON/PMTiles in the repo, where GitHub Pages' ACAO:* and Range support make them free to serve. Do not add a serverless proxy in phase 1; if a must-have source turns out to lack CORS or require a server-set User-Agent, add a single dashboard-pasted Cloudflare Worker (free, no card, 100k req/day, allowlisted upstreams, edge-cached) rather than Vercel/Netlify. Test pure modules with Vitest 5 (fake timers for pacing), add one Playwright 1.63 smoke test in CI against `vite preview`, and verify every API's CORS headers live as the first task once network access opens.
